speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement to the house on the riot which took place yesterday morning at Collins Bay penitentiary, where 441 inmates are held.
The disturbance started at 10.30 while the majority of the inmates were having their morning recreational period in the yard within the prison walls. There had been no advance warning either by rumour, as is usually the case in disturbances of this sort, or by any indication whatsoever. The breakout was sudden, and a number of the prisoners proceeded to set fire to buildings, smash windows, throw pop bottles, etc.
By 10.50 sufficient extra guards had been assembled so that an armed shock troop could be sent in equipped with rifles, tear gas, nauseating gas, and other appliances. Within ten minutes thereafter the riot was under control, and by 11.30 the inmates had been sufficiently secured so that the vehicles of the Kingston fire department and the township fire department could enter the gates and fight the fires. City, provincial and Royal Canadian Mounted Police also assisted in quelling the outbreak.
One hundred and thirteen inmates were actually segregated as those being involved in the riot. During the course of the riot two men were injured. A guard suffered scalp lacerations, presumably from flying glass or a flying pop bottle. One inmate suffered a leg wound which is a flesh wound only. He was wounded when a number of inmates attempted to storm the kitchen and, when ordered to stop, refused to do so. Approximately 12 shots were fired in the air as warning shots, but when the immates still refused to stop a low shot was fired and one inmate was wounded. This immediately stopped the attack on the kitchen and undoubtedly saved an enormous amount of property damage.
An estimate of the damage to the buildings based on information at present available is $52,500. This is exclusive of machinery,
which could not be properly assessed until power was turned on and the machines of various types tested. The buildings damaged were two dormitories, the carpenter shop, paint shop, dissociation cells and minor damage to several other shops. An investigation is under way to ascertain, if possible, the cause of the disturbance and what, if any, further steps may be taken to prevent similar action in the future.
I would like to compliment very sincerely the staff at the penitentiary for their prompt action. Within half an hour after the riot had broken out the inmates were contained. The promptness of the action beyond a shadow of doubt saved many thousands of dollars of property damage and, as it was, for a riot of this size the property damage was small in comparison with other such occurrences. I would also like to acknowledge the prompt assistance rendered to the staff by members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Ontario provincial police, the Kingston police and the local fire-fighting forces, to whom we are extremely grateful.

speechtext: This is a bill to amend the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. The general principles contained in the measure were discussed in the house when the resolution was before it some time ago, and on second reading the bill was referred to the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs. It was very thoroughly considered in that committee and was unanimously endorsed. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AMOUNT PAID TO BENEFICIARY AS ANNUITY, REMOVE RESTRICTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have already given our support to this bill at the resolution stage, and we support it again now in committee. As the minister has pointed out, the bill has been before the committee on veterans affairs and has been very thoroughly discussed. There are, however, a few brief observations which might be made at this time.
The original act, which was passed in 1920, was designed to give insurance coverage to veterans of the first world war and to the widows of those who had been killed in action or who had died of wounds. It was a cheap form of insurance requiring very low medical standards, and it was non-participating; it did not pay any dividends and, of course, it was not negotiable. It was merely intended as protection, not for the veterans but for the veterans' families and dependents.
I wish to bring to the attention of hon. gentlemen some interesting facts brought to light in the committee. The first was that veterans were very slow in taking advantage of this insurance. That is understandable, because at the time they were occupied with getting established and were faced with more pressing problems. In many cases they were saddled with debts and could not afford the premium, but they did become aware of the insurance and took advantage of it when they began building homes and raising families.
The committee was informed that 48,319 of these policies were issued with a value of $109,299,500, and at June 30 of this year 10,570 policies were still in force with a value of $22,362,060. Approximately 12,000 of these policies had been terminated by death, 18,000 had been surrendered, and the balance had lapsed or been converted to different forms of policies.

I think the most interesting fact that came before the committee is that after 40 years the fund is still solvent with a balance of $17 million, and while the government has made contributions from time to time this has been more or less in lieu of interest which has not been charged on the money because this has not been handled in the same way as it would be handled by an ordinary commercial company. Looking into the future we can see that at no time will this insurance be expected to cost the government more than $5 million, since no new policies have been issued since August of 1933.
The changes in this bill are very simple, because they have to do with the payment of claims. The first change merely extends the discretion of the minister to determine the form of payments and the remainder of annuities when they are $1,000 or less; at the present time this discretion extends only to $500.
The other change has to do with substituting the word "contingent" for the word "alternative" as it applies to beneficiaries within the meaning of section 5. Apparently beneficiaries under this legislation were divided into two classes. The original group protected by this insurance were members of the veteran's immediate family, his spouse and children. It sometimes happened that there was no spouse or children living who could benefit; therefore the legislation made provision for a second group of beneficiaries such as parents, brothers and sisters and other relatives who formerly had been described as alternative beneficiaries. Under the amendment the term has now been changed to "contingent". Needless to say we are in favour of these changes and wholeheartedly support this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we of course support this resolution and particularly want to commend the minister and the government on the changes which have been brought about by substituting a new clause 1 in accordance with the wishes expressed both in the house and in the standing committee on veterans affairs.
Bill C-34, of course, is a counterpart of Bill C-33, which we have just passed, and was designed to extend to veterans of world war II the same type of insurance coverage that was extended to veterans of world war I. In fact it went a little further than Bill C-33, because it provided coverage not only for the veterans and for the widows of those who were killed in action or died of wounds, but it included other categories such as merchant seamen, fire-fighters, nursing services and other groups. This legislation became effective on February 20, 1945, and the first policy was issued in April of 1945. Later this same coverage was extended to veterans of the Korean war.
In the committee it was brought to light that up to June 30, 42,508 of those policies had been issued with a contract value of $133,870,000. Of those, 25,523 were still in force on June 20. The maximum coverage under this act is $10,000 as compared with $5,000 under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act, and the average policy issued was $3,000 as compared with $2,000 for veterans of world war II. One of the changes in this legislation parallels the change we made in Bill C-33 just passed, in that it expresses the discretion of the minister on how payments should be made on annuities when the remainder is $1,000 or less.
But unlike Bill C-33 this bill has to do with other changes connected with the issuance of policies and, as the minister has described, the most important of these is the cut-off date with respect to eligibility. Originally eligibility ceased three years after discharge. It was later extended to six years and then to 10 years after discharge; but in 1950 the Department of National Defence amended the National Defence Act by placing on active service not only those who served in the Korean war but the regular forces as well, and this created a problem in that members of the regular forces would, under the legislation as it now stands, be eligible for 10


years after discharge, which would make them eligible to around the age of 60 or 65 when they would, of course, constitute a very great drain on the fund in relation to premiums received and much beyond what the original legislation was intended to cover. This was discussed both in the house and at considerable length in the committee, and a brief was also heard from the Canadian Legion suggesting certain amendments.
I think everybody is in complete agreement that the cut-off date of September, 1962, would be satisfactory, and that it perhaps might tend to hurry up the members of the regular forces who might wish to take advantage of this legislation because experience with this, as with the former returned soldiers' insurance, proves that veterans are inclined to be slow in taking advantage of it and probably for the very same reason. Furthermore, it was felt that people who returned to civilian life should have the same treatment as those who elected to remain in the forces, because actually the people who returned to civilian life would have a much more difficult time getting established and would perhaps have greater difficulty in being able to take advantage of this legislation.
Therefore we are particularly happy to see the changes which have been incorporated in the new clause 1, which extends this legislation to all veterans and, as I understand it, makes all veterans eligible who would formerly have been eligible, up to September 20, 1963.
The other change brought about by this bill will delete section 10, which makes the policy under this legislation much more favourable than under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. Formerly, with section 10, the payment was reduced if the widow of the pensioner happened to be awarded a pension and that, of course, limited the protection afforded by the policy. With section 10 deleted now this will give full coverage up to the face value of the policy.
We are entirely in support of this legislation and taken all together it constitutes what members of parliament and the government have very much in mind, namely the matters which would be of the deepest concern to members of our armed services on their return to civilian life. This was instituted when the original insurance act was passed in 1920, and the tradition is still being maintained, regardless of party, regardless of government, and I am sure that must be a great assurance to all veterans of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, without apologies to the editor of the Globe and Mail I

rise for a second time this morning, and I trust he will not consider that my brief remarks on this most important piece of legislation which is to the advantage of the veterans of Canada are repetitious, unnecessary or inconsequential.
We in this group are very pleased indeed that the minister and the government have seen fit to accept the recommendations of the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs with respect to further amendments to the Veterans Insurance Act. The committee heard representations from the senior officers of the Canadian Legion. After hearing those representations, which I think all members will agree were given with good effect and to advantage before the committee, we had a very thorough and most informative discussion on this whole question. We also received further valuable information from the departmental officials as to the administration of this act. On hearing representations from the Legion and information from the departmental officials the committee, after considerable discussion, made certain recommendations in its report to the house.
Once again I say we are very pleased to see that the government has seen fit to accept those recommendations, which do bring about a considerable improvement to this act. I think these amendments have come at a most appropriate time. As was mentioned here recently, experience with this act somewhat repeats the experience with the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. As the years go by and the date of end of the war recedes, an increasing number of veterans with families growing up have become conscious of the value of this legislation to them. Therefore on that account I think it is most appropriate that the bill has been introduced and a larger number of veterans have been given the advantages that can be obtained under this legislation.
Finally, I would urge all veterans who served in the second world war to give consideration to the value of this legislation and the protection it provides, and on that account to make certain that they all know the details. I suggest to the minister that through some simply drawn pamphlet, memorandum or something of that sort, every effort should be made to inform all branches of the Legion very fully concerning these amendments and when they are to be given effect.

When the bill was discussed in the committee we learned that 1,125 children are benefiting from the legislation, and that the cost as of June 30 last was $885,939.
The committee received a brief from the Canadian Legion suggesting that the legislation should be extended to cover the children of other classes of veterans, particularly those who have died from causes other than their disability, and also even to disabled veterans. It was felt that the legislation was not serving as good a purpose as it might by restricting the benefits only to the children of veterans who have died of causes resulting from their war service.
The committee discussed the matter and the members felt there was possibly a change in principle involved which deserved further study before any recommendation could be

made. We hope that study will be carried on by the minister's department as well as by veterans organizations and other interested parties. I think most of us in this house believe there is a great deal of merit in the suggestion put forward by the Canadian Legion, particularly in so far as disabled veterans are concerned who, because of their handicaps, have not been able to provide as good an education for their children as they might otherwise have been able to do.
We consider this a fairly strong argument, and we do hope this matter will be thoroughly studied. Perhaps at some future date it might be possible to extend the coverage to the children of other classes of veterans.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ALLOWANCE AND EXTEND BENEFITS
speechtext:
Once again without any
apologies to the Globe and Mail for repetition, Mr. Chairman, we in this group support the amendments proposed in this bill. We are glad the government has agreed to introduce these amendments. Possibly there was a lengthier discussion in connection with this bill than in connection with the other two bills in the veterans affairs committee. The representatives of the Legion presented a very complete brief. They had a particular interest in this bill, because I understand it was the Legion who originally proposed this measure. They said on that account they took a keener interest in the operation of the act since it was enacted in 1953. They were particularly glad, therefore, of the opportunity to express their views before the committee and make further recommendations.
After hearing the recommendations of the Canadian Legion, which I thought were very well put indeed with respect to the further amendments they thought were necessary to make this act as effective as it should be, the majority of the members of the committee came to the conclusion that further study was required. I quite willingly admit that these recommendations do introduce certain new features into this legislation, and I quite well understand that members of the committee might honestly come to the opinion that further study is required by the committee, by the Legion and by the government itself.
Personally I gave strong support to the proposals of the Legion, and members of the committee were very sympathetic to those proposals on the whole but were hesitant, generally speaking, about accepting the recommendations without further study. I can well understand that, because while we had an excellent committee a large number of the members had not had prior experience with this legislation, so I can well understand their hesitancy at embarking on something which they did not fully understand. I think

that was the basis of their decision to recommend further study of the suggestions for further amendments put forward by the Canadian Legion.
However, before concluding I do want to say that we were all impressed by the amount of good that is done through this legislation with a relatively small expenditure. I am sure all members of the committee, and all members of this house, recognize the fact that we certainly have a very definite responsibility to the children of those men who gave their lives in the defence of this country. Once again before I sit down, I say that when this or any other government of this country can afford to spend millions of dollars in some cases-I am not objecting to it-to assist in the education or care of people who were on the other side in the second world war and who have since come to Canada because they learned it was a land of opportunity and freedom, we can certainly afford this relatively small sum of money that is required to give effect to the recommendations of the Canadian Legion with respect to this act.
I do hope that as a result of further study of the representations of the Canadian Legion by the government, by members of the committee and by interested people across Canada, next session we will see the minister introducing some further amendments to this act. The amount of good that is done, I think, is remarkable. Therefore particularly in view of that fact we should be beginning to lay the base for wider opportunities for more young Canadians to get a higher education. What better way could money be spent for laying the foundation for wider educational opportunities in Canada for young Canadians than in this type of legislation? I am certain that as the result of an understanding of the results that flow from this legislation, in the near future the government will see fit to extend some similar type of legislation to a wider group of young Canadians.

Right Hon, J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. C-48, respecting the development and improvement of the national capital region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have little to add to that which I expressed on the occasion
National Capital Commission of the introduction of the resolution, except to say that as a result of the suggestions made by hon. members in all parts of the house there was an obvious dedication of the members of this house supporting a capital city worthy of Canada's destiny and of the nation as a whole.
On this occasion, of course, in moving second reading I shall not make any reference to the sections of the bill, except to say that when the original bill was introduced by Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent he simply placed it before the house with a view to having it considered, and also having changes made therein which would be in keeping with the general purposes of the bill and which might be beneficial to those purposes.
As far as the discussion that has taken place is concerned, there was general agreement on the need for improvement of the federal district act, and also a general desire on the part of members to assure that the necessary expenditure will be made in the years ahead to achieve the greatness of a city beautiful. Some mention was made of the plan respecting the city of Washington as an example in that direction. As well, of course, there is the example within the commonwealth of the capital city of Australia, the city of Canberra, where after the area had been determined as the capital of the commonwealth of Australia there have been achieved a planning and a purpose that command the respect of people who visit that great city.
To achieve what we have in mind, of course, will require not only the planning of the commission but the co-operation of the citizens of Ottawa and Hull and the adjoining municipalities, and as well the consideration of the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
I think there is no more for me to say on this occasion except that I believe that out of this bill will come a further expansion and development of the concept of a capital city that was dreamed of by successive prime ministers of this country, one of whom, namely Right Hon. Mackenzie King, gave to the planning a sense of national purpose and dedication which this bill will carry on. All the prime ministers from Sir Wilfrid Laurier down looked forward in prospect to a capital city that would be in keeping with Canada's people, with the contribution of the two major races. All have made their contribution to that end. My hope is that in the years ahead we shall be able to continue the work already under way in making those changes which changing years make necessary while maintaining the general objective that is dear to all of us.
When I look forward a matter of nine years to the one-hundredth celebration of Canada's

National Capital Commission confederation, my hope is that in those intervening years there will be an advance in planning and in the architectural beauty of the city in particular, and that the areas surrounding the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull will see such vast changes that in that year of the centenary celebration we shall have achieved in the main the major objectives and shall have laid the final foundations for this capital city.
Any questions that may arise I shall endeavour to answer, in particular those asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), when we are in committee. In the meantime I shall rest by saying that I ask for the support of hon. members in all parts of the house with respect to this resolution, which I believe is a major step forward and a milestone toward the achievement of that objective which is the aim and purpose of us all.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to delay the second reading of this bill because our views on the matter were expressed on the resolution-that is, our views on the general question-and at that time I mentioned that the resolution introduced by this government was exactly the same as the resolution introduced by the previous government sometime ago. The bill before us now is based on that resolution. We naturally support the purposes of this bill and the ideas and the ideals that have inspired it.
As has been pointed out by the Prime Minister, there is no disagreement in this place with regard to the objective of this bill, namely that our national capital should be one in which all Canadians can take pride. That requires planning. This bill is designed to make that planning more effective than perhaps it had been in earlier days, when I suppose the necessity for planning to make this city a worthy national capital was not as obvious as it has been in recent years.
The Prime Minister mentioned Canberra, the capital of a sister nation in the commonwealth, and what has been done there in the way of planning. Of course the problem there was very different, and perhaps much easier to solve from the point of view of planning, because Canberra was a capital carved out of unoccupied territory and made into a federal district for the purpose of developing a federal capital. That fact must have made it easier for those who were charged with the responsibility of planning that capital, although I know it has also caused some discontent in some quarters of Australia because the capital was divorced to a great extent, by the nature of its location, its development and its planning, from the life of the nation.

It seems to me that Ottawa is particularly fortunate in this regard. It is the national capital, but it is also a Canadian city taking part in the life of Canada, not merely in the life of the government of Canada. We are fortunate in that respect and fortunate also, as so many hon. members have said, in the beauty of its location, which provides the planners with something on which to work; beauty unsurpassed by any capital in the world. This planning which is required and which will be facilitated by this act is one thing, but if it is to be successful, government buildings in the national capital must be worthy of the plan. This means that even the most functional government buildings will have to reflect those aesthetic qualities which the Prime Minister so rightly mentioned as being desirable in the development of a national capital. This applies to government buildings on both sides of the provincial boundary. It would certainly be unfortunate if we concentrated on building good and beautiful government buildings on one side only and ignored, to some extent at least, the same requirements on the other side of the provincial boundary in Quebec.
There is a great deal that needs to be done before this city can be made into a worthy capital, and we are all conscious of projects that need to be carried out. There are many corrections to be made which could have been made so much more easily if the work of planning had been begun 25, 30 or 40 years ago. However, this bill is now before us. It is one with which I think we can all agree. It means that we are approaching another stage in the development of a national city which will be worthy of our great country.
It is well when we consider these matters and talk about planning to look a long distance ahead and not be too much influenced by short-range considerations. We have suffered from that in the past in this country and in this capital. The Prime Minister will recall, as a student of history, that when the east block and west block were originally constructed some of the public men of that time deplored the extravagance, and I remember one famous Canadian saying that the day would never arrive when we would have enough government business in this country to necessitate the occupation of those two monstrous palaces, the east block and the west block.
That was not so long ago, less than 100 years. So it is well to remember that when we plan for the future we should plan for the day after tomorrow, not for tomorrow. As we do that I think we will be able to look back on this bill, as I have said, as another stage of this plan to make Ottawa the kind of capital that Canadians would like to see.

I
wish to assure the Prime Minister from the outset that we welcome this bill most heartily. We see it as an attempt to strengthen the hands of those who are devoting their interest to the development of a truly national capital of which all Canadians can be proud.
We have looked over the bill, and in the main we feel that the provisions of this measure will do exactly what they are intended to do, namely strengthen the hands of those who will be charged with this responsibility. I notice that toward its end this bill repeals a previous act, and I hope the Prime Minister can assure the house that after the passage of the bill now before us there will not be any undue delay before making the declaration that is necessary, because sometimes, with the demise of one corporation there is a considerable lapse of time before the new corporation begins its activities.
The need for national development is so urgent that I hope the present act will not remain in existence very long, but that all haste will be undertaken to proceed at once with the new arrangements. Those presently responsible will naturally hesitate to undertake many necessary measures if they do not know exactly how long they are going to be in charge of their responsibilities. For this reason I hope the proclamation will not be long delayed.
I should like the Prime Minister when he replies to indicate the reason for the omission of section 20, as it was in the old act, calling for an annual report to parliament. I notice nothing in the new bill which calls for an annual report. I know full well that parliament will have an opportunity to discuss the work of the new national capital commission whenever it is asked to vote funds. However, there may well be a period of a year, or possibly of several years, when no additional moneys are being asked for and in that case there might be no convenient way of parliament taking under advisement the activities of the commission for a particular year. I feel there should be something in the bill which would enable parliament to discuss each year what has taken place.
In the main, though we support the principle of the bill, we wish the measure had gone a little further in some respects. I will possibly have a little more to say on that when we come to discuss the various clauses. There seems to be spelled out rather severe limitations on the actions which the commission may undertake; the limitations on real estate dealings are somewhat severe. Very far-reaching authority is exercised by the governor in council, in some ways possibly greater authority than obtained under the old act. I hope this is a safety measure only,

National Capital Commission and that the cabinet has no intention of regarding itself as, in effect, the new national capital commission. As I say, I notice that very little which is of major consequence can be done without the approval of the governor in council.
I regret that the commission is not being given a little more authority to aid the municipal corporations. These municipalities within the federal district, especially as now defined, have heavy responsibilities. If, as the Prime Minister indicated, nine years hence on our one hundredth anniversary as a nation we are to have in the federal district cities of which we can be truly proud, a terrific responsibility is imposed on our municipalities, and I am not sure that the act as it now stands will enable the commission to give the financial assistance which a city such as Hull, for instance, would need if it is to make the progress which I am sure it would like to make within the period of the next nine years. I should like to have seen a little more authority given to the commission to aid the city councils financially in order that they might make their cities into the type of cities we would all like to see.
I also hope the Department of Public Works will work in very close co-operation with the new commission, and that when the department undertakes any project within the federal district it will take into consideration whatever representations the national capital commission will have to make. I refer particularly to the type of buildings and the location of buildings undertaken by the department. I hope the Department of Public Works will not operate as an autonomous and independent organ in putting up buildings in the new federal district.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words on this matter. Everyone seems to be satisfied with the changes referred to in the house today, because the old act was really no longer sufficient to meet the needs of the national capital in the development of the general appearance of the region. Recently many hon. members and possibly the Prime Minister as well have received communications from two bodies on the Quebec side of the national capital.
One of those concerned recommendations about the name of the governing body. In the old days people were not happy about the word "district" appearing in the name, because it created the impression that it was the intention to make of this area a district similar to the district of Columbia in the United States, which has proved an unsatisfactory arrangement from the point of



National Capital Commission view of those living there because that commission decides on the development which is needed and the expense and then undertakes it. The United States government pays a certain part of the cost and the balance is said by the local population through the imposition of taxes. The people there are attempting to persuade the United States government to change the present arrangement that obtains in the district of Columbia.
I know it was never the intention of the government to have obtain here the situation that obtains in the United States capital, but I also know that a minority of Canadians feared that result because they did not understand the intention of the government, and of course we cannot prevent people from being afraid.
The official name of the measure before us is the national capital act, so there is no connotation of a region or a metropolitan section. It looks to the people outside the city of Ottawa and to others as though the act refers just to the city of Ottawa itself. I know this is not the intention of the government and never has been its intention, but because of the representations recently made to the Prime Minister and to some if not all hon. members I know some associations would be more at ease if the name could be changed by adding the word "region" or "metropolitan".
This would tend to lengthen the name, but it is fashionable today to refer to organizations by their initials instead of their full name, and this would not represent too great a change. It would serve to give the people living outside the limits of the city of Ottawa a feeling that they are really included in the national capital development plan, and that all improvements made under the plan would serve to benefit them as well as the residents of the city of Ottawa.
I am pleased that under the present bill the moneys to be spent by the commission will be voted by the house. With the limited amount the commission had to spend in the past it was restricted to a certain amount of work, and we could expect it would have taken a very long time, perhaps even a hundred years, to complete the plan which was prepared under the supervision of Mr. Greber. The moneys will now be voted by parliament, and a good start has been made.
The government has voted $20 million for the green belt around the city of Ottawa; and because buildings and bridges come under the purview of the national capital commission I wish to take advantage of that situation to ask the government when voting money under the new act to include a sum for a new bridge to replace the present

atrocity between Ottawa and Hull known as the Alexandra bridge. If we delay until agreement is reached among the federal government and the two provincial governments it will be a long time before the bridge is replaced.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I trust the hon. member does not intend to pursue that matter, because it is not strictly on the principle of the bill.

No, Mr. Speaker, I simply wanted to refer to the improvement in the appearance of the area the replacement of this bridge would achieve. I hope the government will see that money is voted to enable the commission to correct this situation.
A matter of concern to residents of the city of Hull that has been discussed at length in the past is any attempt that might be made to do away with the E. B. Eddy Company. Some people seem to think that a factory of that kind is an eyesore. The company has considerably improved the surroundings of the mills, and it is really not unattractive. It serves to show visitors to Canada that industry can exist in close proximity to the national capital without detracting from the beauty of the locale and it is an example to visitors of one of our most important industries.
Not long ago I was speaking to the wife of the ambassador of France to Canada. She told me that she considered the plant a beauty spot because it demonstrated the possibilities and potentialities of our country, and I share that view. I hope the new commission will make no attempt to remove from the city of Hull its main industry. We are all in favour of aesthetics, beautiful parks and scenic roadways, but we should also be in favour of industry which continues to help people earning a livelihood.
As the E. B. Eddy Company is the most important industry in the city of Hull we want it to remain where it is. We can continue to effect changes and improvements in the surroundings such as have been taking place in the last ten years. I have from Mr. Weston the promise that he will continue to make the surroundings more attractive to those visiting the city. I express the earnest hope that the commission will be requested by the government to make no attempt to remove this company from the city of Hull.

Mr. Speaker, before the Prime Minister speaks in closing this debate I should like to raise one matter very briefly, and that is the omission of any requirement in the bill for an annual report to parliament by the corporation. I should like to ask him, since we have almost reached the luncheon adjournment, if

he would examine this question and, unless there is some very good reason for the omission from the bill of such a provision, to consider the matter with a view to having such a clause added to the bill so we could have it for consideration in committee this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the Prime Minister speaks now he will close the debate.

I have just a very few words. I thank hon. members for their contributions. I do not intend to deal with the several matters raised by them at this time, except the question raised by one hon. member to the effect that government buildings in this city should be in keeping with the national capital plan. I am informed by the Minister of Public Works that all government buildings receive the approval of the federal district commission as to architecture and the like, and also the extent to which the buildings will fit in with the planning of the federal district commission.
When my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition referred to the beauty of Ottawa I could not refrain from mentioning how often I go over to Hull and when there look across to the city of Ottawa, for there is no more noble or inspiring silhouette anywhere in the world than the parliament buildings and the buildings associated with government administration as seen from that city.
Two hon. members mentioned the question of an annual report and asked why this had been omitted from the present bill. The reason is that under this bill the commission is an incorporation under the Financial Administration Act, and under section 85 of that act an annual statement is required to be made to parliament. Therefore any fears that any member may have that an annual statement will not be placed before parliament are entirely met by the provisions of the act to which I have made reference.
As to the other questions that have been raised may I say this. All of them are worthy of consideration and all of them will receive the attention of the new commission, but I do offer a word of advice. It would be somewhat out of keeping with the responsibilities that rest upon that commission if the government endeavoured to dictate to it in any way as to the manner in which, within the ambit of its powers, it will carry out those responsibilities under the act.

speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the other day the hon. member for Ottawa West asked a number of questions, and I shall deal with those questions in the order in which they were asked. Some reference was made to the financing of the new commission, and at page 3363 of Hansard the hon. member asked the following question:
Will the Prime Minister say something at this stage about the method of providing the financing; that is, the necessity for funds which will be in the nature of capital and which will not lapse at the end of a financial year and the provision of the operating funds for the annual maintenance work.
Section 16 of the new act provides for the new financial arrangements. Operating expenses of the commission, including maintenance of parks and parkways and of grounds of government buildings, will be financed by an annual vote of parliament.
Capital expenditures will be financed by payment into the national capital fund each year of amounts appropriated by parliament. The fund will provide for construction and other projects undertaken by the commission and also for the commission's share of approved projects which may be undertaken in conjunction with municipalities and other public authorities. Expenditures for lands not immediately required for projects will be financed by loans. Amounts credited to the national capital fund each year will not lapse but will be carried over from year to year.
The hon. member's next question was:
Then I should like to ask him about the commission itself. He will notice that when the previous bill was introduced by the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, in 1957, a good deal was said about the operations of the commission itself; that is, how it was proposed to be set up. I wonder whether the Prime Minister would feel free to tell the committee just what he envisages in that respect?
My answer to that question in general is that the composition of the commission and of its committees is dealt with in clause 3 of the bill. Then there was a question regarding Ottawa river pollution, as follows:
If the Prime Minister is in a position today to tell us-I do not know whether he is or not-I would ask him to tell us what he can about the participation of the federal government in that scheme.
The answer is the mayor of Ottawa is asking, through the federal district commission, for financial assistance from the government. That matter is under consideration. As the hon. member knows, the report of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of

National Capital Commission Commons in 1956 drew attention to the need for cleaning up the Ottawa river, and indicated that the problem is essentially one for the two provinces and the municipalities concerned, but further suggested that because of the national capital interest the federal government should give a measure of assistance.
Pollution is caused by a number of Ottawa sewers which empty directly into the river, and to a lesser extent by sewers of Quebec municipalities. The Ontario water resources commission has recently directed the city of Ottawa to take steps to construct a disposal plant to handle sewage from Ottawa, Rock-cliffe and Eastview. Following this, the city engaged two firms of consultants to design a disposal plant and also an intercepting sewer system. These reports were received in June, 1958.
The recommended plan is the same in principle as that contained in the Gore and Storrie report of 1949. It includes a disposal plant at the mouth of Green's creek, several miles east of the city, and an interceptor sewer 7J miles long extending west from the plant to a point near the Chaudiere falls. The cost of this interceptor, which will connect the various existing sewers which now discharge into the Ottawa river, is estimated at $11,800,000.
The hon. member went on to say:
When this work was carried on by the Ottawa improvement commission, at one stage it was thought that the south boundary of the city was in what is now the centre town section and the driveway system, which we are all proud of now, extended along what is now Clemow avenue and Monkland-
-and so on.
My answer to the hon. gentleman's rather lengthy remarks, which appear at page 3364 of Hansard, is that if something can be carried out along the lines indicated as between the commission and the city with regard to Clemow avenue and Monkland avenue the government will be glad to make the necessary, suitable approaches to the province in that connection.
Then the hon. gentleman referred to parking meters on Wellington street. Wellington street, of course, as the hon. gentleman knows, is a city street and the installation of parking meters is a matter for the city. I would suggest that he direct any views he has in that regard to the city authorities.
The hon. member also asked what main projects were in mind that would require a substantial expenditure of money in the immediate future. The main projects which the commission has undertaken in recent years and which are still being continued are the railway relocation scheme, shared projects with municipalities, for example the Queens-
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
way, park and parkway development and the green belt. The details of proposed expenditures on capital projects in 1958-59 will be found in the commission's capital budget as tabled in the house. The long-term forecast of possible expenditures over a period of years on various projects is contained in the brief submitted by the federal district commission to the parliamentary committee in 1956 and is printed in the proceedings of that committee.
The final questions of the hon. member were based on these statements by him as found at pages 3364 and 3365 of Hansard of August 11:
In 1947 expropriation proceedings were started with regard to properties along the Ottawa river with a view to completing the driveway system along the river in a westerly direction from the centre of the city . . . Work also required to be done to develop the driveway system along the south and southeast shore of the Rideau river.
I may say that I feel sure the commission will desire to give sympathetic consideration to the representations regarding the initiation of parkway construction along the Ottawa and Rideau rivers and also the continued development of Sussex drive; but expenditures for this purpose will, of course, have to be considered in the light of the very substantial amounts required in the next few years for the railway relocation and other construction projects.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

There are just one or two more questions I should like to ask. First of all I should like to thank the Prime Minister for the answers he gave to the questions I asked when this legislation was at the resolution stage. I wanted to add one or two remarks about the questions and answers.
On rereading the questions I think I might not have made clear the point I had in mind concerning Clemow avenue and Monkland avenue. At the time the commission preceding the federal district commission was active, that is the Ottawa improvement commission, they had undertaken certain restrictions and certain provisions in connection with the area now covered *by these two city streets, Clemow avenue and Monkland avenue. With the passage of time these streets have become regular city streets, but the federal distict commission is still burdened with their care and maintenance. There is some legal difficulty about having the city take over these streets.
I believe anyone examining the matter would consider it desirable that these streets

be given back to the city for care and responsibility. The only legal way in which that end could be accomplished, as I see it, is through the provincial legislature. My question was merely directed to asking the Prime Minister, if and when the matter came up with the federal district commission or the new national capital commission, to use his good offices to have the province take the necessary legislative action to vest the appropriate parts of that land in the city.
The second subject matter, I believe, had to do with parking meters on Wellington street. I was referring, as I think the Prime Minister will see, only to that part of Wellington street immediately in front of the parliament buildings. While I very much appreciate the Prime Minister's answer on the point, I am going to ask him to pursue the question a bit further. I think he will find in old agreements and records that work was done by the public works department on this street. I hope the Minister of Public Works will not mind if I give him some research work to do, but I believe it will be found the federal government does have some responsibility for work on the north side of Wellington street, mainly in front of the parliament buildings. I think he will find also that part of the land close to the Chateau Laurier is the responsibility of the Department of Transport.
I should like to be a little persistent and ask the Prime Minister to pursue this matter further and settle, once and for all, the question of title to that land with a view to having that part of the north side of Wellington street properly maintained. I for one cannot easily reconcile myself to having this beautiful site on which these buildings are located spoiled by car parking. Indeed, I could say a great deal more about car parking on the hill itself, but I am going to leave that part aside for the moment.
I believe it is important that we not let anything be done now by the city that would tend to mar the beauty of the site of the main parliament buildings. I recognize that with the Prime Minister as busy as he is it is not always possible for him to concern himself with things that may, in themselves, appear like small matters. I do feel quite strongly on this matter, however, and I would ask him to have the appropriate officers look into the matter and do what they can to prevent this further step being taken that would mar the beauty of parliament hill itself.
Then the third matter I want to raise has to do with the annual report. I listened to the Prime Minister's answer to my request earlier this morning that he consider putting a provision in the legislation requiring the commission to make an annual report to
National Capital Commission parliament. As I understood it, his answer was that there is a provision in the Financial Administration Act requiring crown corporations to make a report to parliament on their finances. I am aware of that provision, but what I have in mind is something quite different. I have in my office copies of annual reports of the federal district commission for quite a number of years. These are very fine reports. They contain a great deal of information that does not concern financial administration at all.
If the Prime Minister will look at these reports I believe he will be impressed with their excellence, and I think he will be impressed with the important information they contain describing developments in the national capital, the beautification of the area and the development of the national capital area throughout the years, as well as the projects pending for the coming year. These reports usually contain some maps and pictures, and altogether the reports are very commendable.
I feel quite sure, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members would wish to have copies of such reports in future. I would ask the Prime Minister, notwithstanding the answer he gave to this same point this morning, to reconsider this matter and put a provision in the legislation requiring an annual report.

I thank my hon. friend for his suggestion, Mr. Chairman. As I said this morning, the commission being a corporation under the Financial Administration Act, an annual statement is required. I believe his request is reasonable. Each year the report has been a compendium of much useful information, and I shall suggest to the commission that the annual report made under the provisions of the act include the type of information that has now become characteristic of those reports. As a matter of fact, under the bill prepared by the former prime minister this section had been omitted for the reason I gave. However, I shall see to it that the purpose the hon. member has in mind will continue to be before the new district commission in the making of annual reports.

Before one o'clock the Prime Minister said that whenever there was a building to be erected in the capital region, the plans were submitted for the approval of the commission. This has been the practice for years, and I feel it is a very good thing to do. If I were to go to the commission and ask them to do something about the Hull side, somebody might say I was interfering with the business of the commission.

National Capital Commission
I should like to ask the Prime Minister, therefore, that the new commission consider spreading the money around a little more so we would have some buildings on the Quebec side. At the moment the plans call for buildings being erected miles away from this House of Commons. There are some beautiful sites on the other side of the river, and these buildings would then be much closer. I know we have one building there now which has been criticized quite a lot, and I will come back to that on another occasion. This was recommended in 1949 by the commission to the government; the recommendation was accepted and they started to buy the land to build the printing bureau, which has been a great improvement. As is stated in the report:
The plans had been prepared for this new imposing building, the construction of which will commence the gradual rehabilitation of a part of the city of Hull, which is now blighted. The building will be accessible from all sides by direct arteries-
And so on. So they found a place which was quite suitable for a building, one of the important ones. If they can find-and I know they can-other suitable places in Hull or in the surrounding area much nearer to the parliament buildings than some of the new buildings which are being built at the other end, I think it would be to the advantage of those working there; it would be advantageous to distribute more adequately the circulation around the city of Ottawa. It would be advantageous also for the park area, and it would also help to change parts of the city of Hull which are very old.
The city of Hull was built as time went by, and some of the houses which are there were built by people working at Booth's, Eddy's and other places where they could get wood very cheaply. They built those houses at night in order to get dwellings in which to house their families. Those buildings are old, and in certain areas they could be bought at a certain price. If this were done it would help to improve the surroundings of the city of Ottawa, and it is still in the national capital plan.
So I hope the commission will accept the suggestions I am making today through the Prime Minister and have a little bit more sympathy for the city of Hull and the Quebec side of the national capital surroundings. I hope if they happen to need the money for that purpose, the government will be large enough to vote the money. Parliament will be large enough, but I hope the government will be satisfied to recommend the expenditures which might be asked for by the commission. As they were saying, the printing bureau building will be accessible from all sides by direct arteries.


I hope we will come to the decision that for the betterment of the national capital another bridge will be built to permit traffic to circulate. At the present time many of the population want to go to Gatineau, that beautiful national park beyond compare with any other in the world. If they want to go there they need to cross the river. In order to cross the river they need a bridge. The bridge situation is really bad. The only way it can be done is through the national capital commission. I hope they will recommend to the government the building of a new bridge, and I hope the government will recommend the expenditure of the money.

In connection with the reference just made by the hon. member for Hull, may I say this. In the bill that was tabled by the former prime minister, Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, he will find that section 9 provided as follows:
There shall be an executive committee of the commission consisting of the chairman, the vicechairman and three other members to be appointed by the commission-
I felt that did not cover the situation properly having regard to the representations that should be made on the part of the people of the province of Quebec and the city of Hull. It was with that end in view that the bill before us has these additional words:
-of whom one at least shall be from the province of Quebec.
That was an additional change that was made by this government in order to assure that proper representation would be made in connection with the executive committee.
On this question I shall have to tell the Prime Minister that there was always a member from the province of Quebec.
Oh, no.
It was Mr. Amyot from Quebec who was the member representing the province. We had Mrs. Fontaine representing our side, and we had the mayor of Hull at that time.
This is the executive committee. There were no representatives on the executive committee.
I will admit they were not members of the executive committee, but they were members of the commission.
Oh, yes.

Under the bill there is one person representing the city of Hull, where we had two, and there is one representing the outside of the city, which is an improvement on what we had. I think that makes 16 altogether. There are still four who can be

nominated at any time. I hope when those four are nominated, another one will be nominated for the area surrounding Hull or the city of Hull.

I am curious about the Prime Minister's answer. I do not understand why he should single out the province of Quebec? Why should he not have provided that the province of Ontario should at least have one, or the city of Ottawa? I just want to point out that the principle being followed in legislation, in designating one particular area, is sometimes a difficult one to administer and is not perhaps as attractive in principle as it sounds. Perhaps he should have put in a provision that at least one shall be from the province of Ontario, or two or three or four or twelve, as the case may be. That is a very doubtful principle to follow, though I can appreciate the hoii. gentleman's motives in putting it in.
Does the hon. gentleman want that change withdrawn?
I do not know why the Prime Minister would want to put me in a spot like that, but I am sure the people of Hull would not mind if it were withdrawn. I do not think this really adds anything at all-
They asked for it.

-one way or another to this bill. Anyway, the point I want to make is that this is a doubtful precedent to set, because once you start that kind of thing there may be provision for at least one representative from Rockcliffe Park, or the province of Ontario, or the Gatineau area, and so on; and I am sure the hon. member for Carleton would wish there to be a representative from the county of Carleton and that the hon. member for Russell would wish a similar provision to be made for Russell. So we would go on.

Mr. Chairman, I think more expropriation could be done on this green belt. All your railways and what you call the station and everything else will be in the Russell riding. Alta Vista drive and Elmvale Acres are among the nicest parts of the capital of Ottawa, and they are near where the station will be. Therefore it has to be something to go with this nice part in my riding.
However, I am not afraid, because I am sure there will be some intelligent people representing the city of Ottawa on this commission; it will be easy to get good ladies and good men to become representatives on the board. And I point out to the Prime Minister, when he is talking about the beauty of Ottawa, that it is hard to compete with the beauty of
National Capital Commission the district of Russell. When members talk about Ottawa and talk about Hull let us not forget that there is no better area than Eastview, with 23,000 people and some of the best buildings that anyone could wish to see.
I am quite certain that the good wishes of all hon. members here will go with this board, and that it will be prepared to continue the good job which has been done up to now. I hope that in carrying out this task it will soon be able to improve the approaches to this city by building a bridge starting from the north in Hull to the south on Sussex street in Ottawa, and also one further down, which would be another link between the provinces and enable the Quebec people to come to Ottawa and the people of Ontario to go to Quebec.
Does the hon. gentleman for Ottawa East agree with that?
The hon. gentleman from Ottawa East always agrees when it is a good thing. He is a bright fellow.

I guess I would agree to anything which would improve the Ottawa East portion of the national capital area. I am not expecting the Prime Minister to make an announcement at this time about the program of building along Sussex street, or to tell us when the tracks are to be removed. I think I have been in this game long enough to know that the Prime Minister will require some time to become acquainted with all the problems of the capital area before he can tell us.
However, this would have been a wonderful occasion to have announced that the bridge from the end of Sussex street to Hull was going to be built by the federal government. I think everyone would be happy to hear that, and I think if we keep on repeating it, within a short time we will hear an announcement made by the Prime Minister on the subject. I believe that when he does so he will receive the plaudits of all hon. members here.
Another question I should like to raise concerns transportation in this city. I should like to know if negotiations have been held between the federal government and the city of Ottawa on this question, and whether the Prime Minister is aware of any such negotiations. I should also like to ask whether any proposals have been agreed upon, because everyone knows that the displacement or removal of federal buildings from the central part of the city-the greatest offender being, of course, the Minister of Public Works and his predecessor-into the lovely riding of Russell has disturbed the living habits of the people of the city of Ottawa and made transportation very difficult.

National Capital Commission
As a result the city is now facing a transportation crisis, and I think the only solution lies in an agreement with the federal government so that in the future the city may be advised in advance of the government's plans regarding buildings, knowing that if it does provide transportation in such cases it will receive compensation and that the city and the citizens of Ottawa shall not be the losers.
As I said the other day, it is not always an easy problem for people to live in the city of Ottawa. It is an expensive process, and the taxpayers of Ottawa have paid their share toward the beautification and improvement of the city. I hope this transportation problem will be one of the matters which the government will attend to as quickly as possible in an effort to reach a suitable solution.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Definitions.

Mr. Chairman, under 2(i)
the following definition is given:
"Minister" means the Prime Minister of Canada or such other member of the Queen's privy council for Canada as is designated by the governor in council.
Now the commission is answerable to the Prime Minister of Canada, and I merely want to ask the Prime Minister if he proposes any change by the definition given in this section.

As the hon. gentleman
knows, in the bill that was presented by Mr. St. Laurent the minister was defined as the president of the Queen's privy council for Canada, or such other member of the Queen's privy council for Canada as was designated by the governor in council. There is no change in this regard, and there is no change contemplated. As a matter of fact, though I am Prime Minister I have never been sworn in as president of the Queen's privy council, and I presume that is one of the reasons why this was phrased in its present form.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Prime Minister would permit a question purely for information. Did I understand him to say he had not been sworn as a member of the privy council?
No; as president.
Oh, he meant he was not sworn as president; I see.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3-National capital commission.

Mr. Chairman, this morning I referred to the communications which had been received by hon. members of this house and the Prime Minister from various organizations on the other side of the river in the

province of Quebec concerning the name of the commission. The official name is the national capital commission, and I wonder if there would be any serious objection to naming it the national capital region commission or the national capital metropolitan commission. This involves just the addition of one word to the title, and would satisfy many people who fear the name is restrictive and bears reference only to the city of Ottawa. It should be easy to change the name along the lines I have suggested without detracting in any way from the project involved.

Mr. Chairman, that
matter, of course, received consideration at the time the committee sat in 1956. I do not think any one would read a sinister meaning into the expression "national capital commission". The fullest consideration was given to that matter. This is, indeed, the national capital. For that reason the commission received that name. There may be a time when further consideration could be given to it, but at the moment I believe it will be generally agreed that the name is one that actually covers the connotation intended.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say how much I welcome subclause 5 of clause 3 which places a limit on the length of time any member may serve; a maximum of eight years, as I understand it, unless it be the chairman. This will automatically provide new blood in the membership of the commission every once in a while, which I think is a good improvement.
I notice in subclause 3, however, a change from the previous provision. The corporation of the city of Ottawa and the corporation of the city of Hull used to have the right to appoint a member of the commission. I regarded that as being of some value in establishing a liaison between the two city councils and the commission. Has the Prime Minister any explanation to offer as to why that provision has been eliminated; why all members of the commission are appointed by the governor in council and none are to be direct appointees of the city councils?

When this matter was being considered it was felt that the previous provision served as a handicap to the commission. Under the Federal District Commission Act one member was appointed by the city of Ottawa and one by the city of Hull. These have usually been the mayors of the respective cities. It was felt in consideration of this problem that in view of the frequent negotiations with the cities it is a handicap to the commission to have representatives of the cities at its meetings. The new act provides for the appointment by the governor in council of at least two members

of the city of Ottawa and one from the city of Hull, and one from a municipality in Ontario other than the city of Ottawa and one from a municipality in Quebec other than the city of Hull. That was the consideration that prompted the inclusion of this particular subclause.

I wish to ask the Prime Minister if he has any explanation to offer as to how proper liaison will be maintained between the city councils and the commission if there is no direct tie-up between them. I know he said the commission was perhaps handicapped in having direct representation -as he said, the mayor-however, I fail to appreciate how one man could embarrass the opinions of the other 19 members of the commission. I am afraid we may have developed as a result of this move a lack of that understanding which is so vital if the work of the commission is to be at all successful. How does the Prime Minister propose to maintain the necessary liaison?

There are frequent meetings of the chairman and general manager with the mayor, and between the staff of the commission and the staff of the city. I am sure there will be no lack of liaison or of representation to achieve a proper relationship and to assure that the views of the city will at all times be given full consideration by the commission.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 4 to 8 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 9-Executive committee.

Mr. Chairman, I fear I did not make myself clear previously when speaking about subclause 1 of clause 9. I should perhaps read this subclause. It reads as follows:
9. (1) There shall be an executive committee of the commission consisting of the chairman, the vice chairman and three other members to be appointed by the commission, of whom one at least shall be from the province of Quebec.
I am concerned about the last part of that sentence containing the words "of whom at least one shall be from the province of Quebec". Those words were not included in the bill that was introduced by the former government. The Prime Minister has offered an explanation as to why he caused those words to be added, but I would point out to him that it is a doubtful principle he is following in putting in this special reference to one province and not the other, because it is now quite possible to have this executive committee without any protection for the national capital.
Under the British North America Act Ottawa is the capital of Canada. That is a
National Capital Commission statutory provision, although there are occasions when I feel some may have forgotten it. This started out as an Ottawa improvement commission. It grew to a federal district commission and now to a national capital commission, a move which I think all persons welcome as an indication of progress which we all commend.
Approximately 12 years ago we provided that on the federal district commission there should be representation from each province in Canada, which was evidence of the growth of the country and an increased appreciation of this program. Now, because of the difficulties inherent in having meetings attended by members of the commission from each province in Canada, it has been found necessary to create an executive committee.
I wish to be clear that I am perfectly agreeable to having a representative from the province of Quebec on the committee. I hope there will be no misunderstanding on that point. I believe it is a requirement any sensible person would have in mind in setting up the executive committee, and I am wholeheartedly agreeable to the idea. But if we are going to legislate on this question, then surely we must also include a provision to the effect that of the three other members to be appointed by the commission, one at least shall be from the city of Ottawa or one at least shall be from the province of Ontario.
We should not have discriminatory legislation in this form on the statute books, and I am sure the Prime Minister would be the first to agree to that principle. I suggest to him that he add the words "and one at least shall be from the province of Ontario". It is a principle that is worthy of the attention of the committee and of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to support what my hon. friend from Ottawa West has said. The national capital region, of course, is in two provinces, namely
Quebec and Ontario. It would be normal_______
indeed it would be desirable, perhaps essential-that on any executive committee there should be members residing in those two provinces. I assume that normally would happen, but in this legislation provision has been made to ensure that it will happen in the case of only one province. We all agree that it should be so for that province, but should not exactly the same action be taken in respect of the other province, as suggested in the amendment that my hon. friend from Ottawa West has ventured to put forward?

May I differ a little with the proposal made by the hon. member for Ottawa West. The idea of the bill as it stands is to have a representative from the Quebec region. I agree with the hon. member for

National Capital Commission Ottawa West that it looks a little discriminatory when we say that one shall be from Quebec and we do not mention the other nine provinces. It can be freely admitted that if it were changed to read that one at least should be from the Quebec side of the national capital region there would be no misunderstanding. As it reads now somebody could be taken from the city of Quebec or from any other part of the province, and he would be too far away to attend meetings of the executive committee.
What the Prime Minister wants, I believe, is to have somebody on the spot to be there when they need him at executive committee meetings. The bill as it stands provides for a member from every province. We find that in clause 3. If the idea is to have a representative from the Quebec side on the spot it would be much better to have it read "from the Quebec side of the national capital region".

Mr. Chairman, a little while ago the member for Ottawa West, possibly speaking without that care which he might have exercised, placed this section giving the province of Quebec representation on the executive committee in a position similar to that of the various municipalities. He said, if the province of Quebec is to have a representative why should not municipality A, B, or C have one? There has been no request whatever from Ontario for any specific representation on the executive committee; there was from the western Quebec boards of trade, which asked that in the setting up of this executive committee provision should be made for a representative from the province of Quebec.
I felt that was a reasonable view because of the inclusion in the national capital region of those areas that are administered by the commission. It was to cover that point that this specific reference was made. I must say that I felt that was proper and fitting, and I still do. I feel there should be representation from the province of Quebec. When the hon. member for Hull says that representation on the executive committee should be from the region in question, I can assure him that this is the area from which the representation will be taken.

Mr. Chairman, may I make myself clear. I think everybody in the house agrees that there must be representation on the executive committee from the province of Quebec. Certainly I did not intend to create any other impression. I for one cannot see any possibility of an appropriate executive committee which did not have representation from the province of Quebec; but what I am pointing out is that in doing so we are creating


a situation where there might not be any representation from the province of Ontario, and the national capital happens to be in the province of Ontario. I think we should keep our sights on the main objective of this legislation, namely the creation of a national capital commission.
I do not want to delay the proceedings unduly, but I would again request the Prime Minister to add wording which would provide also that there be at least one member from the province of Ontario. I think it would be found on examination that this is a reasonable request; it is sound in principal and it is practicable and possible. Without being too persistent, I would like to ask him to consider the matter again and also to consider adding the appropriate words at the end of clause 9, subclause 1, which will provide that at least one member must be from the province of Ontario as well as one from the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, the national capital executive committee would naturally have representation from Ontario. We are not going to set up an executive committee and then appoint the members from various other parts of Canada. This executive committee will be an operative committee. It is natural, in the nature of things, that it will be largely composed of those immediately in the area or environment. Having that in mind we felt as well, because of the extension of the district into the province of Quebec, that we should assure that on the executive committee there should be a representative from the province of Quebec.
The Leader of the Opposition says it is discriminatory. That observation surprises me. I see nothing discriminatory in providing that on an executive committee which deals with the national capital we provide for a representative from the province of Quebec. There is nothing in the nature of discrimination there.

Just so there will be no doubt as to where I stand on this matter, I think the Prime Minister has already said in his last few remarks that there cannot in fact be discrimination because there will always be a member of the executive committee from Ontario. If that is so, and undoubtedly it is so, why not put it in the law? It also is the case that on an executive committee of this kind there will be representation from Quebec. We all understand that, and we all approve it. That has been made clear in the legislation by including the words "of whom one at least shall be from the province of Quebec". Then, as long as those words are included in the legislation and no reference

is made to the province of Ontario, whatever the situation may be in fact-and there will undoubtedly be no discrimination in fact- there is the possibility of discrimination in law, and it is merely to remove that possibility, so there will be no misunderstanding in the future, that my hon. friend has suggested that this very useful and simple amendment might be made to this particular clause.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 10 agreed to.
On clause 11-Co-ordination of development.

I should like to refer to subclause 5, but to make my point I must read subclause 4, which is in these words:
No person shall erect, alter or extend a building or other work on public lands in the national capital region unless the site, location and plans thereof have first been approved by the commission.
I think subclause 4 is very necessary. However, then we come to subclause 5, which reads as follows:
In any case where the commission does not give its approval under this section the governor in council may give such approval.
What I am a little afraid of is that this provision may lead to undue influence being exerted on members of the government. I believe the commission should have the final authority. If the work of the commission is not satisfactory then, if the charge is serious enough, the commissioners can be removed from office. After all, they hold office only at the pleasure of the governor in council.
