I do not like to see a situation where a person who is refused permission to undertake the construction of a building on national capital region land can then exert political pressure in order to reverse the decision of the commission. In my opinion this is a weakness in the clause, and I should like to hear what the Prime Minister has to say.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that I see no reason for the suggestion that in the exercise of this power political pressure would be exerted against the governor in council. As a matter of fact, my hon. friend's solicitude in this regard would indicate to me that he has in mind examples of political pressure having been applied. If he has not, then I would point out to him that this particular subsection has been in effect since 1946.

I realize that it has been in effect, but I do not believe that members of the cabinet should have to be bothered with people appealing to them to do what they can to reverse a decision of the commission.
National Capital Commission I feel that the commission members should have the authority to carry out their work, and that if anybody has received an adverse decision he should not have the right to appeal to the government to upset the decision of the commission.

I must say that is a somewhat new doctrine. I have always held the view that when money is appropriated by parliament the government must assume the responsibility for the expenditure of that money, and I would think the government cannot escape that responsibility under our legislation.
I rose to bring up this point. Ever since 1946 it has been the law under the Federal District Commission Act, in wording almost identical to that of the new bill, that when any public building is to be constructed in the national capital area the site, location and plans thereof must first be approved by the federal district commission, now to be known as the national capital commission. That has been a very useful provision. It has done a great deal to co-ordinate the development of the whole national capital area. It has meant that the exterior design of public buildings has had to be co-ordinated and made compatible with the characteristics of the general site and location of the buildings.
I should like to be assured by the Prime Minister, as I have no doubt is the case, that no change is contemplated and that it is the intention to follow the same practice that has been followed in the past of insisting that the section be meticulously observed with regard to all public works undertaken in this area. I must say that this sometimes carries with it decisions that are not always happy for some of us, but I would point out to hon. members that as far back as April 30, 1949, at the time the national capital committee documents were tabled in the house, a full page story appeared in the Ottawa Citizen in which there is reference in item 14 to the construction of a new government printing bureau to be located in Hull.
I do not want to get off on that subject, but I would point out to hon. members what is involved in these things. It means that the site of these buildings are chosen with a view to the development of the whole national capital area, and we must bear that in mind. Further reference to that subject will be found in the national capital general report of 1950, page 210.
The government is also Involved in another way. Because of the aesthetic requirements of exterior design, many of these government buildings may be more expensive than they would otherwise be. I think it is desirable to place that fact on record now

National Capital Commission so that hon. members will understand exactly what they are legislating when they approve this clause. I think it is a wholly appropriate provision, but one that is not widely understood by hon. members, and I should like them to know and appreciate just what it involves. I hope that decades from now there will be many people in this chamber who will thank us for having put this provision in the legislation initially in 1946, and for having carried it forward in the 1958 legislation.

Mr. Chairman, clause 11 reads in part as follows:
(1)	The commission shall, in accordance with general plans prepared under this act, co-ordinate the development of public lands in the national capital region.
(2)	Proposals for the location, erection, alteration or extension of a building or other work by any person on public lands, or by or on behalf of a department, in the national capital region shall be referred to the commission prior to the commencement of the work.
I do not want to go back to what I said a while ago, but I hope the commission will consider very favourably the Quebec side, which is much nearer the main buildings of the government, when dealing with proposed buildings to be erected for the benefit of different departments.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot agree that it is necessary for responsible government that subclause 5 should remain, even though it has been in the old act; because there are many crown corporations as to which the cabinet would not entertain for a moment any representations concerning their internal operations. The Prime Minister mentioned the possibility of the old subsection 6, now subclause 5, having been used. I see he has an adviser in front of him, and I am wondering whether the Prime Minister can inform us how often subsection 6 of section 9 of the old act was used in years gone by. I am not asking for the exact number, but has much use been made of the right to appeal to the governor in council in past years? I should like to have an indication of how much use has been made of the provision.
I can only speak of the period since I became Prime Minister. No use has been made of that subsection during that period, nor has there been any application for its use.

I notice that throughout this bill there is mention of plans. I should like to repeat what I have said before in this house, that I believe everyone would welcome the day when we have a definite plan. At the moment there is no plan approved by the municipalities involved or the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I feel


that that is what is lacking in our approach towards this national capital development. We have not got an approved plan, something which shows what the commission intends to do. A person may settle 20 or 25 miles from here and within a few years find that he is involved in expropriation proceedings because a new plan has been made. I believe that, as soon as possible, we should have a plan approved by all concerned which would be made public so that the people who live in this region would know what to expect so far as their property is concerned.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 12 agreed to.
On clause 13-Expropriation.

I have some remarks to make about expropriation. My good friend the Prime Minister will appreciate the point of view I have always taken that there should be a review of the Expropriation Act by the Minister of Justice. This is a very severe act. The purpose of this act, when it was put on the statutes, was to acquire property on behalf of the crown for public works, works of necessity such as wharves, post offices, defence projects and so on. At the moment the same strict regulations or sections which were applied for this purpose in the past are being used under such statutes as this one. I have always felt that there should be some amendments made to the Expropriation Act for use in such cases as the national capital plan.
Some people do not appreciate what is the procedure. It only requires a plan to be signed by the national capital commission and filed at the registry office, without any notice to the owner of the property, for property to become vested in the federal district commission. The rules in connection with compensation are those that existed in the past for ordinary expropriation purposes such as the public works I mentioned. These procedures are very lengthy and slow. The people of Ottawa have suffered from these procedures in the past. I know that in recent years the commission has not been using the Expropriation Act to the same extent, and hardly at all on the Quebec side. I know that in Ontario this act was used to acquire almost all the property along the Ottawa river and a great deal in Russell county. I believe this is the time to revise the Expropriation Act, and I hope the Prime Minister will give some consideration to discussing this matter with the Minister of Justice.

In practice, Mr. Chairman, the commission follows the course of endeavouring to purchase the property by

agreement rather than by expropriation. What the hon. gentleman says is a fact, that the power of expropriation being an extraordinary one deserves to be reconsidered in the light of present circumstances. I can tell him that the Department of Justice is reviewing the Expropriation Act in detail with the operative departments to the end that anything in the nature of enforced injustice cannot occur.
In saying that, I do not admit that there has been such in the past. Nonetheless, the power being so extraordinary, it certainly should be limited so far as possible. I should like to point out this to him. I do not believe most powers of expropriation-I am speaking now from memory of the law after not having practised for two or three years-have the limitation that is present here. Here, the commission may, with the approval of the governor in council, take or acquire lands for the purpose of this act without the consent of the owner. In other words, if expropriation takes place within the national capital region, it can only take place if the governor in council has directed that it should take place.
Mi;. Mcllrailh: All the authorities for expropriation are that way.
I have to admit that the claim of the hon. member for Ottawa East is correct to some extent. I remember one case where an old man was expropriated-
Oh, oh.

The hon. member may laugh, but if he had to struggle in French as I have to struggle in English he would not dare laugh at me that way; that is very cheap.
This man was over 65 years of age, and they wanted to expropriate his property. He was living on a small pension, and they gave him the exact value of the house. This man had no money to rebuild and the cost of construction had increased to such an extent that he could not do anything. He could not even buy a lot. It is quite important that the Expropriation Act be revised so that these poor people would not be disturbed for the balance of their lives.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 14-Restrictions on transactions.

I notice a change in clause 14. Where the terminology "at a price" was used in the former bill there is a change to "for a consideration". Is there any special significance in that change in the new bill?

One can imagine a situation whereby a trade would take place, whereby a certain piece of property in possession of the commission might be exchanged for another property of equal value.
National Capital Commission It was in order to cover that situation, as I understand it, that the word "consideration" was inserted.

I looked at this clause, Mr. Chairman, and I was wondering why the figures were so low or limitations were so severe. It seems to me that very little can be done by this commission without an order in council. They cannot dispose of any real property if the value is in excess of $10,000, nor may they buy any real property if the value is in excess of $25,000. That means that the greater number of transactions will require orders in council. Does the Prime Minister have any explanation to oiler as to exactly why $10,000 and $25,000 were the figures used, as to why the provision was not made a little bit more liberal or why a little bit more leeway was not given to the commission to act on their own, as for example up to $25,000 for disposal and $50,000 for purchase? In these days it does not take much of a home to be worth $25,000. Surely we do not want an order in council for each and every house.

It is apparent, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member has not read the Federal District Commission Act. The old section 16 reads as follows:
16. (1) No separate parcel of real property shall be purchased or acquired by the commission at a cost in excess of five thousand dollars except with the previous consent of the Governor in Council; and if the commission is unable to agree with the owner of real property as to the price to be paid therefor, the commission shall, with the consent of the governor in council, have the right to acquire the same without the consent of the owner and the provisions of the Expropriation Act are, mutatis mutandis, applicable to the acquisition of such real property by the commission.
There was that provision in the past respecting $5,000 in the acquirement of property. It was felt that provision constituted too great a limitation on the average transaction. The change that has been made is this. Under the Federal District Commission Act the commission cannot dispose of any real property without the approval of the governor in council. Under the new bill the governor in council approval will not be needed unless the consideration involved exceeds $10,000. Under the Federal District Commission Act to which I have just made reference the commission cannot acquire a parcel of property in excess of $5,000. Under the new bill governor in council approval will not be needed unless the consideration involved exceeds $25,000. It was just to cover the point raised by the hon. member that this alteration was made.

I want to assure the Prime Minister that I have read the old act.

National Capital Commission
Then I apologize to the hon. member.

The point I was making in my opening remarks is that I feel that all around the commission is being limited a little bit too much, that it is not being given enough freedom of action to do the effective job that the Prime Minister wants it to do in the nine-year period.
I must say that the first time in my life that I ever heard the Prime Minister make a public speech was in the little village of Craik, Saskatchewan in the year 1941, I believe it was. One of the most telling arguments that he had against the government of the day was the vast number of orders in council that were being issued. Knowing that he has so little love for government by order in council I should have liked to see in this clause and in other clauses evidence that the new commission about to be appointed would have a little bit more liberty of action.
The effect of the alteration will be to reduce the number of orders in council, that desirable objective to which the hon. gentleman gives his adherence now.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 15 agreed to.
On clause 16-National capital fund.

Would the Prime Minister care to tell us what supplementary estimates he proposes to bring before the house this year dealing with this subject? I have in mind particularly the question of whether or not he proposes bringing before the house provision for funds for acquisition of part of the green belt.

Authority will be asked for a $4J million loan on behalf of the commission for green belt purchases. In addition to that, of course, there will be these other estimates to which reference can be made when the estimates are before the house.

What I want to point out is this. The expropriation legislation provides that payments shall be made at the value at the date of expropriation. Once the expropriation plan is filed the persons concerned have by that time had the valuations of their property fixed. If you are in a period of rising prices, great hardship is suffered by those persons because the crown does not have the money with which to pay them the value of their property. If they have no other assets, they cannot buy other property and they are left in a rather hopeless position. They know they are being put out of the existing property, if it is property that is being taken for


use. The price is fixed as of the date of filing of the planned expropriation. The crown cannot pay them; and if the values go up, of course real hardship is suffered. There has been a great deal of hardship on that score. The hardship has been quite severe. All too many persons are suffering in this area because they have had their property expropriated. They have had no payment made by the crown. The value is fixed as of the date of expropriation. The situation can work a real hardship. Now that the green belt is announced and the delineations of the border fixed by the publicity given in the last few weeks, I would ask the Prime Minister if he would consider providing funds so that these expropriations can be completed as quickly as it is mechanically possible to do so.

I wonder whether the Prime Minister could indicate to the committee what has been the cost to the taxpayers of Canada of the development of our national capital so far? I know that for many years certain amounts have been voted annually. I wonder whether we might have the figure of what has been spent so far?

According to the report as of March 31, 1957, which is the only one I have before me at the moment, the funds advanced to the commission have amounted to $21,540,000 and the total expenditures have been $21,054,991. There have been further expenditures, of course, during the period 1957 to 1958 but I have not those figures before me at the moment. I will have them when the estimates are before the house.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 17 and 18 agreed to.
On clause 19-Regulations.

There is a small legal point that I should like to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister. Clause 19 (1) provides for the making of regulations for the protection of the property of the commission and for preserving order or preventing accidents. Then the remaining subsections of the clause have to do with a vehicle being operated or parked and so on and provision for penalties. What I want to point out to the Prime Minister is this. I want to ask him whether he is satisfied with the wording of clause 19 (1) in its breadth, from the point of view of giving authority to make regulations controlling traffic. The authority is quite clear for preserving order and for preventing accidents; but there can be control of traffic that is not protection of property and that is not preventing accidents. I do not want to delay the passage of the clause now in order to discuss the point further, other than to draw the

matter to the attention of the Prime Minister and to ask him to have the appropriate law officers look at the clause and, if they find anything in the points raised, have an appropriate amendment put in possibly in the other place or at some other convenient time.

At first glance, Mr. Chairman, I am inclined to think that there is something in what my hon. friend has said. However, I wish to point out that this clause was drafted in its present form by the Department of Justice after receiving full information respecting the requirements of the R.C.M.P. relative to these matters which come under the jurisdiction of that body. The purpose is that which the hon. gentleman has in mind-infractions of that nature, in addition to other provisions-the protection of property and the like. If it were not for the fact that the law officers of the crown concluded that this would be sufficient, I should be inclined to agree completely with the hon. gentleman, and I am not going to disagree with him now, even having regard to the authority of those who have prepared this. If he has any suggestion as to an additional word which would correct the situation, I would certainly be glad to accept an amendment in this regard.

I am not going to set myself up as a legal authority in a committee such as this, but the Department of Justice has been known to overlook points of law on occasions-I say that without any undue reflection on that department-and it seems to me that authority to the governor in council to make regulations concerning the control of traffic is not given by this section, although regulations are obviously intended on this subject, because subclause (a) of (2) deals with regulations concerning the operation and parking of cars. Perhaps we could let it go at this point, and the Prime Minister will have them take another look at it.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 20-26 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 27-One and same corporation.

I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in the bill introduced in April, 1957 by the former government there was a provision that the corporation referred to in section 3 as the corporation established by the Federal District Commission Act was hereby declared for all purposes to be one and the same corporation. This was followed by a somewhat lengthy subclause which provided that the persons who held offices as chairman, members, officers or employees of the federal district commission immediately before the coming
National Capital Commission into force of the act shall be taken to have been appointed or employed to be chairman, members, officers or employees of the commission respectively under the new act for the unexpired portion of their respective terms to which they were appointed or for which they were employed. And then there is further provision for carrying this out.
That provision has been totally eliminated from the new bill now before the committee and the effect of it is that if the bill passes in its present form the members of the commission, the officers and the employees of the federal district commission are immediately out. They would require to be reappointed or rehired and by the mere passage of this bill and the bringing of it into operation that is the consequence. It means that the men who maintain the grounds around the city-indeed, those who maintain parliament hill and do all this excellent work- are left in a position of total insecurity of tenure of their employment although their work may have been such as to bring about the commendation of all of us. I should therefore like to ask the Prime Minister if he would explain just why this subclause 2 was omitted in the new legislation, and precisely what he has in mind.

As the hon. member has stated, Mr. Chairman, this was in the draft bill which was introduced by Mr. St. Laurent. It was unusual, I thought, for such a provision as that to be made in this type of legislation. No one wants any person to be left in a position of total insecurity. Provision has been made in the bill that it shall come into effect on proclamation, and I can certainly assure the committee that the omission to include this provision was based on the fact that in the past a section such as that had been significantly omitted from legislation passed by the former government, and the reasons given were simply that in order to assure that the act should be most effective, while accepting in general the provisions of the draft act, we do not feel that positions should be filled by inheritance or by statute.
There is plenty of support for that stand in legislation passed by the former government.

I wonder if I might pursue this matter a bit further. Would the Prime Minister give us an example of some of the legislation of the previous government where the name of a statutory body was changed and some changes were made in its powers, and when this provision or a corresponding one was omitted? I cannot recall any.

I would have no difficulty in that connection. Let us take 1936, when the

National Capital Commission department of mines and resources was reconstituted by the statutes of Canada, chapter 33. That was passed on June 23, 1936. That is one example. The hon. gentleman must have forgotten that the Federal District Commission Act took the place of the Ottawa improvement commission in 1926-27. This change was brought about by the Federal District Commission Act, the act for which the present bill is being substituted. That act is reported in chapter 55 of the statutes of Canada, 1927, the act cited as the Federal District Commission Act. Section 21 of the act constituting the Ottawa improvement commission-chapter 10 of the statutes of 1899-and the act continuing the said improvement commission-chapter 62 of the statutes of 1919

were repealed and the provisions of the later act substituted for that act and the amendments thereto. Now, that was a pretty good example but there is still another one, the Canadian broadcasting commission.
Corporation.

This act succeeded the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission Act. It appears as chapter 24 of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1936. I believe the Canadian Broadcasting Act covers the situation very completely. Section 25 of that act reads as follows:
The corporation shall, from the date of the coming into force of this act, take possession of all property and assets and assume all the obligations and liabilities of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission.
Section 27 provides:
The Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932, chapter 51 of the statutes of 1932, is repealed.
Section 28 reads:
This act in whole or in part shall come into force on a date or dates to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council.
And then there is the act respecting national parks, chapter 33 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1930, passed on May 30 of that year, and there are similar provisions although, as far as this act is concerned, one might say there is a distinction because like the first mentioned, those were acts respecting departments of government. The government felt it would prefer to follow those outstanding examples introduced by the previous government rather than the drafting prepared by the last government.
Mr. Chairman, there are one or two comments I feel 1 should make about the answer. First of all I would point out that the Prime Minister was obviously prepared for this.
I read about it in the Ottawa Citizen.

I congratulate the Prime Minister on that but I am just wondering what caused him to be so prepared on the point. What has he in mind? He must have been thinking about this subject. I would also point out there are employees who worry about this in a very real way and have every reason for doing so.
I should also indicate that two of the four pieces of legislation to which the hon. gentleman referred dealt with civil servants and have no relevance whatever to the discussion before the committee today and for that reason should not have been referred to at all. One referred to the Canadian broadcasting commission-
Corporation.

-and one referred to the Ottawa improvement commission. I am not familiar with the former. I must point out the substantial nature of the changes being made with reference to the Ottawa improvement commission. There was no change of government at the time the legislation was put through. It was being continued under the same government. I wish to draw that to the attention of the committee.
I wish to point out to the committee that the subclause that is omitted deals with the officers of the commission. That is one group of persons. But then it also deals with employees of the federal district commission.
I	think it should be impressed on hon. members that some of these employees of the federal district commission hold humble jobs but they have been there over the years. These were not patronage appointments and they do not benefit through the civil service commission.
This is a proper occasion on which to ask the Prime Minister whether he proposes to make any changes in the commission itself. If so, is he in a position to tell us what the changes are? Secondly, when he deals with that part of the section, will he then tell us about the employees and include some provision in the bill that will protect those employees as well as the officials and members of the commission? In other words, there are two groups of persons referred to in the subclause that has been omitted. I feel it is quite an important thing. The commission has developed in a highly successful way over the years. I cannot help but be impressed with the attitude of all hon. members of the house toward the commission. If you read the debates on the subject for the last decade that will become extremely apparent. We heard what was said on August
II	at the resolution stage and we have heard the fine words spoken from all sides of the house today. I for one am not content to see

a somewhat glaring omission like this in the new legislation that will create the suspicion that there are going to be mass dismissals of employees and mass rehirings. I believe the Prime Minister ought to consider making a firm and definite commitment on this subject.

Mr. Chairman, I would point out that when the C.B.C. was set up under the new act in 1936 no provision was made similar to that which Mr. St. Laurent in this case thought should be included, a rather unsual provision and one that naturally must have won his appreciation and support. As far as the commission is concerned, there are certain terms expiring December 31, 1958. There are six members whose appointments-and those six include the mayor of the city of Ottawa-terminate at that time. Then in 1959 there are a further six commissioners' appointments expiring on December 31. One expires December 31, 1960.
In so far as the employees are concerned, no employee or official who is discharging his responsibilities in a way befitting the position he has occupied will ever have anything to fear whatsoever. I wish to make that very clear and very definite.
When the hon. gentleman speaks about the glaring absence in this section, I must say that in so far as two of the cases to which I referred are concerned, the course followed there represents the course followed generally. After all, when a new body is set up naturally those who are doing their work in a proper, fitting and efficient way will have no cause for concern.

In view of what has happened I am not sure that my hon. friend deserves the congratulations of my hon. friend from Ottawa West for having done his preparatory work so skilfully. He produced four illustrations to support his position, two of which dealt with civil servants and are completely irrelevant, one of which my hon. friend dealt with. He was able to show the difference between that particular operation and this one. The fourth is relevant. It deals with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but it goes back to 1936. My hon. friend says that the provision which Mr. St. Laurent would have included in his bill, and which has been cited, was an unusual one and that the government now proposes to follow the normal and usual course in this matter.
I would suggest to the Prime Minister that perhaps the reason he did not cite any examples to support his case from the end of world war II was that he was not able to find any relevant examples. I suggest also-he will correct me if I am wrong-
National Capital Commission
Have any changes been made?

-that what the Prime Minister considered to be the unusual provision, the one that Mr. St. Laurent put in, was not unusual and was in fact the one that was followed since world war II when changes of this kind were made.
However, perhaps we can bring this matter to a head and get from the Prime Minister the kind of assurance that we would like to have by asking him to state, if he cares to do so, that the position of the members and employees of the new commission in regard to their security of tenure will be exactly the same as if the section quoted by my hon. friend from Ottawa West, which would have been included in any bill from this side, had been included in this bill. In other words, their position will not be affected in any way by the fact that that provision is not included in the bill and they will be treated in that way notwithstanding its omission. I suggest again, Mr. Chairman, that the inclusion of such a provision would not have been unusual. If the Prime Minister does some more homework he might find that it has been included in more than one bill since world war II.

I ask the Prime Minister not to put himself in a position where he may be tempted, but to put something in the bill which will help him to resist the temptation of some of his members who may try to play politics. I suggest that he have some kind of regulation that will isolate him against temptation of some of his members to have some of the employees released because they were appointed by another party. It will save him a lot of trouble and a lot of temptation.
I might also remind the Prime Minister, if he does not remind himself, that he has found his desk very handy. Two weeks ago he spoke of removing desks. If he did not have his desk in front of him he would not find it so convenient to have all those books in front of him. I ask him to forget about the desks because they are handy for everybody.
The books were under the desk.

I ask my good friends to include a provision so that there will not be a temptation to put some of the employees out of jobs because they were hired by the Liberals. I think it would help to have a regulation along that line and it would prevent the Prime Minister from running into a lot of trouble.

Mr. Chairman, of the two acts referred to by the Prime Minister one

National Capital Commission was passed 32 years ago and the other 22 years ago. The bill that he proposes not to follow is one that was introduced one year and four months ago. I wonder why he selects the one passed 32 years ago and omits the one introduced 16 months ago. It does not make a very good case. I would point out also that while he tells us about the date of the expiry of office of many members of the commission he does not go any farther in discussing the clause with which we are dealing, nor did he deal with the unexpired period of the duration of their appointments. May I ask him directly now to deal with that omission? Is it the intention to reappoint the members of the commission when the new act is passed for the unexpired term on the dates he indicated in his statement a few moments ago?

That matter has not yet received consideration, but in the appointment of the commission under this new act the only consideration will be the efficiency and the effectiveness of those to be appointed.

But we have had some rather extraordinary tests of efficiency given to us in the house. We had one the other day by the Minister of Transport in dealing with the auditors of the C.N.R. It was a shocking definition of efficiency, and I would like the Prime Minister to be a little more clear on what he means by that. I would hope he would use the same test of efficiency that some of us would use, and if he does we will be satisfied. I would be much happier if it was in the legislation, but if it is not in the legislation dealing with the commission would he consider, in view of what he has said, putting in a clause dealing with the employees only, similar to the former clause 2?

Mr. Chairman, the form in which the presentation has been made and the removal of this subsection-and also the change in at least half a dozen or more other subsections and sections of the draft act that was tabled by Mr. St. Laurent- represent the stand of this government on this particular question.

Mr. Chairman, I have been listening very carefully to what the Prime Minister said, and it has occurred to me to wonder whether there was ever in any legislation as early as 1936 any provision of the character suggested by Mr. St. Laurent in this bill. I suggest the reason that there was nothing that the Prime Minister found at that early date is that this kind of situation at that time was, to say the very least, abnormal.


My recollection is-and I am speaking from recollection; I may turn out to be mistaken; I know I am taking a very great risk in speaking from recollection-that when the national film board was established during the war and it took over the employees of the motion picture bureau of the Department of Trade and Commerce, some special provision was made for the security of the employees who previously had been in the civil service and who were then being transferred to this new crown corporation. I do know of my certain knowledge that since the war when, for example, the department of reconstruction and supply was first being set up and taking over the employees of the department of munitions and supply, and again when the department of reconstruction and supply was wound up and its employees were taken into certain departments that were taking over, provision was made for the continuity of employment of the employees.
I know from experience I have had that there have been many, many cases in which similar provisions were made in so far as employees were concerned, and here I am only referring to the second point raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West.
So far as the members of the commission are concerned, if the government wishes to drop that provision in the previous bill I would have no criticism at all. It would seem to me that the government was perfectly justified in doing that if it wanted to. But with respect to the employees there are many precedents going back in my recollection to the establishment of the film board where, when a new name or new constitution was given to some agency and functions were transferred from a department to a crown company or vice versa, legislative provision was made to safeguard the position of the employees.
It would take me some time to look up and verify the references but I have very distinct recollections of having dealt with these matters myself and I know that there were such provisions. I would not like to say, of course, that they were in the precise language to be found in the bill Mr. St. Laurent introduced but I do know that it has been habitual and normal since the war to do so. Therefore, while I would not urge the government for one moment to do it with respect to the members of the commission, so far as the employees are concerned I would urge them to do what has now become and has been for some 15 years the normal practice in these matters.

Mr. Chairman, I would point out again the whole history of this legislation. We have had a national capital development authority operating in this city and area since the late 1890's. It has gradually developed over the years and has come to be a very fine body whose work is recognized and appreciated throughout the country. As a logical consequence of all their work a joint committee of parliament was set up in 1956 to deal with this whole subject. Resulting from the work of that committee legislation was drafted and brought in but was not proceeded with in 1957 because of the dissolution of the house and the calling of a general election.
Similar legislation has now been presented by the present government. During that time not only has the work of this body come to be appreciated throughout Canada but the house itself has come to recognize this subject as a non-partisan one and the commission as a non-partisan commission in all its works, with all the implications of the word "nonpartisan". Today we have this splendid piece of legislation spoiled by the omission of the one clause providing for continuity of employment for the employees. That is something that should not be done. A clause providing continuity for the employees should be included in the bill. From anything the Prime Minister has said I cannot understand why such a clause should not be included at least so far as the employees are concerned. I would regret it very much if the committee were to pass this clause in its present form and by that one act undo so much of the splendid work done over the years, work that has been recognized in all parts of Canada. Notwithstanding the firm position the Prime Minister took a moment ago, I would ask him to consider putting such a clause back in the bill at least so far as the employees are concerned.

Mr. Chairman, since the Prime Minister has suggested what attitude I should take to a precedent established by Mr. Mackenzie King, I say here and now that I yield to no person in the house in my admiration for Mr. King, but if I were seeking a lawyer I would certainly ask the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent for legal advice before I would ask Mr. King, and so would Mr. King.
I say that the statutory precedents, the numerous precedents, the dozens of precedents, for protecting public servants in legislation brought into the house by Mr. St. Laurent impress me far more than something that happened 22 years ago when the situation was quite different at the very beginning of the Liberal regime of Mr. King. I think that the Prime Minister should reconsider, and give this group of public servants the same protection as was given to the employees of the motion picture bureau when they went to the film board, the same protection that was given to employees of the Department of Finance who went to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the same protection that

National Capital Commission has been given as a normal procedure when these transfers have been made because of changes of this character ever since the war and, indeed, over the last 15 years. That is all we on this side of the house are urging. That is what Mr. St. Laurent intended to do and that is what the government is proposing not to do.

I asked the Prime Minister a few moments ago, because I thought this might clarify the discussion, if he would give the committee an assurance that the security of the positions of the employees of the commission will be the same as if this section, which had been proposed by Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, were included in this legislation. If he could give us that assurance, it would certainly go a long way towards settling our doubts.

I thought I covered the situation completely, and I am surprised the hon. member did not follow what I said. I said positions are not filled by inheritance or by statute. What I want to assure above everything else is that the efficiency and effectiveness of this body shall be completely unimpaired.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 28 agreed to.
On clause 29-Commencement.

I wonder if the Prime Minister could give any indication as to the commencement of this act? After listening to the interchange which has just taken place, I think it is obvious that possibly not all the members of the commission under the former act will be members under the new act. There may be, therefore, some hesitancy about doing anything about the development of the national capital pending the proclamation of the new act. I think all of us would regret six months of inactivity or perhaps a year might elapse before the act is proclaimed.

My hon. friend must have been thinking about the past when he uttered those concluding words. The purpose is that at the earliest possible date the proclamation will be made. This date, of course, must be fixed with due regard to the necessary preparations that have to be made to bring the act into effect. I have no hesitation in saying, however, that I believe there should be no delay beyond that which is necessary to assure, as I said a moment ago, efficient and effective service.

Clause agreed to.
[Mr. Pickersglll.l
On the schedule.

We have now a new definition of the national capital region set out in this bill. We have a new green belt. A map has been published and a description of the area. However, I am wondering if the Prime Minister would consider having the mapping section of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys prepare a comprehensive map showing the national capital region, the green belt and all the other relevant data pertaining to this legislation. There is a need for it. While the federal district commission did some excellent map work, they were of necessity limited in this work. We have this outstanding branch of the government service that could do the work, and I would ask the Prime Minister to consider having that branch prepare a comprehensive map with all the relevant data on it.

I think that suggestion is a very good and appropriate one. As a matter of fact, I have found difficulty myself in trying to follow the actual areas in detail of these various entities. While I have no authority to direct, I shall certainly bring to the attention of the department of mines the need for the preparation of such a map. I think it is necessary. As the hon. member said, there is bound to be confusion without it.

Schedule agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-49, to provide for the conditional liberation of persons undergoing sentences of imprisonment.
He said: I should just say a word or two on the second reading of the bill. 1 will not go into any detail because I think I gave a sufficiently comprehensive outline of the general principles and purposes of the bill when the resolution was before us, as reported on page 3372 of Hansard for August 11, 1958. I should just say, in addition, the following: This bill which is now in the hands of members deals with a system of parole under

which persons undergoing sentences of imprisonment may be conditionally released to serve the balance of their sentences at large in society. In considering a bill of this nature, therefore, some consideration must be given also to the purposes of imprisonment.
The purposes of imprisonment are generally regarded as being twofold: firstly, the punishment of the offender and secondly, the rehabilitation and reform of the offender. In so far as the first part, namely the punishment of the offender is concerned, we are not immediately concerned with that here except to the extent that no one having overall responsibility for penitentiaries could altogether overlook the punitive aspect of imprisonment. But apart from that indirect concern, we are not here concerned with the punitive aspect of imprisonment but are concerned with the design and implementation of a program of rehabilitation and reform of those who have been sentenced to penitentiary.
While those who administer the parole system which will be set up as a result of the passage of this bill will be primarily concerned with the question of whether a prisoner is qualified to be released on parole, nevertheless it will be their responsibility also to concern themselves indirectly with questions of the rehabilitation and reform training programs in penitentiaries as well as with provision for assistance of those who are released on parole. The purpose of this bill is to provide for the setting up of a system which we believe is generally in accord with the recommendations and findings of the Fauteux committee, and which will assist in a sensible, constructive and valuable program of rehabilitation and reform of prisoners, and their return to society as useful members of society in the shortest possible iime consonant with the overall responsibility of those in charge of the penitentiary system lor the protection of society. This is the ourpose of the bill, and I believe that as ion. members study the bill in detail, they vill see that we will be in a better position o discharge and perform this purpose under he new bill than we were under the Ticket >f Leave Act which this bill repeals and eplaces.

Speaker, I feel quite sure it is not neces-ary for me to make any lengthy speech on he second reading of this bill to indicate to he minister that we on this side of the house Till support the measure. Of course we shall iave the opportunity of asking questions and lerhaps voicing minor divergences of opinion

as to the details of the bill. Generally speaking, however, we are in agreement with and concur in the general principles involved in this particular bill.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, all the suggestions to be found in the Fauteux report of 1953 are indeed timely and to the point. We feel that they are well worth reviewing and studying from time to time. One of the important recommendations of the Fauteux report, of course, deals with the parole system in Canada. I understand this recommendation will be implemented in great part by the passing of this bill. I feel sure that there is not a member in the house who has not, at one time or another, been faced with representations from mothers or wives in respect of the imprisonment of their loved ones. There are times when the circumstances under which the imprisonment has taken place, the state of mind of the imprisoned persons and also the deplorable conditions of the family, the wives and children, would argue very strongly for the conditional liberation of certain prisoners. Although we are warranted in commending and can very well commend the remission service of the Department of Justice and while we can also commend highly the present Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) and the former solicitor general, we feel that this whole system was working under a very heavy handicap. It is hoped that this new bill-and I think it will do so-will bring about conditions where it will be far easier to deal with parole.
The Ticket of Leave Act passed in 1899 is, of course, completely inadequate and out of date, and it cannot cope with circumstances and conditions which have been brought about by our modern society and by our social psychology, if you wish to call it that, which inmates carry with them into the remotest corners of our penal institutions. We feel that in many instances it would be perhaps to the great advantage of the prisoners as well as of society to be in a position to offer rehabilitation to many of the prisoners rather than to have them serve their full sentences or their full terms. I think this is particularly true of the younger inmates, young men and women who are just a little bit older than those whom we consider to be juvenile delinquents. I feel that they perhaps need rehabilitation more than they need punishment. I sometimes believe that their plight is due to the way of life that we have chosen to live, with its very materialistic philosophy. I sometimes feel that somehow we may be responsible for creating in the lives of our young men and women psychoses of many sorts. I believe that we should, particularly at this time, try to rehabilitate to a greater extent in many cases rather than to punish.

National Parole Board
For this reason I think that the creation of the national parole board in the form of a quasi judicial body could make possible a far more competent and complete examination of the circumstances and conditions surrounding the imprisonment of an inmate. I also think this body would certainly be in a better position to judge of the effectiveness of granting parole to certain prisoners. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house propose to vote in favour of this bill.
There is, however, a question that arises in my mind as I read the bill. If the present legislation, namely the Ticket of Leave Act, is to be repealed and to be replaced by the parole act, are we to understand that the Solicitor General will join the ranks of the unemployed in this country?

subtopic: REPEAL OF TICKET OF LEAVE ACT, ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak for a very few minutes on this measure. I again say that the members of this group are pleased indeed that the minister has given effect to the recommendation of the Fauteux report with respect to parole by the introduction of this bill. I think there is no question that it is a definite forward step in the administration of justice in the humane sense and in the rehabilitation of persons who have transgressed the law. I am particularly interested in this matter because during my experience in this house it has been brought clearly to my attention what could be done to rehabilitate persons who, through unfortunate background-home life in some cases and associations-have committed serious crimes.
Since I have been here I have always found that those responsible for the administration of the Ticket of Leave Act have done the best they could under the provisions of that act. I remember on one occasion a man wrote to me. He had lived in Trail during the war. I never met the man. He asked for remission of sentence. In his letter to me he said that he had been an ardent supporter of mine and that he believed in the C.C.F. policy, particularly on the question of the socialization of the banks. I went to see Mr. Ilsley about the matter, when he was minister of justice, and he very kindly agreed to look into the matter thoroughly. About two weeks later he called me into his office and he showed me the record. He said to me, "Mr. Herridge, I think there is no doubt about it; this man does believe in the socialization of the banks. He has been going ahead with that work quite extensively in recent years". It was his third bank robbery. Therefore on that occasion I did not proceed any further with my representations on behalf of this to me unknown person. However, I mention 
that as one little humorous incident in a number of what, over the years, have been tragic incidents for the persons concerned.
In recent years throughout Canada there have been a good number of people and groups who have taken an increasing interest in the rehabilitation of persons who have transgressed the law. I am sure that those who take an interest in persons of this class do so for purely unselfish purposes. It is one of those aspects of society in which persons are interested because they have some sense of brotherhood so far as their fellow man is concerned and some sympathy for those who have fallen by the wayside.
I want to make one point before sitting down because I am a great believer in getting support for the law and for its administration.
I am quite sure the minister would agree with me that sometimes his officials have not been able to do all they would like to do because they lacked the normal public support in the performance of their duties to meet certain serious problems.
I suggest, therefore, that if this measure is to be fully successful it must receive the co-operation and understanding of each section of the public in this country, and in this connection I should like to read one paragraph from the report of the committee which was appointed to inquire into the principles and procedures followed in the remission service of the Department of Justice of Canada. This paragraph struck me very forcibly. It appears on page 54 of the report, and it reads as follows:
Finally, it is clear to us that education of the public is essential in order that proper parole principles and procedure may become better understood. Unfortunately one parolee who violates the conditions of his parole often receives such widespread publicity that the whole system appears to be defective.
I am sure that many members of the house would agree with this from their own experience.
Usually overlooked, of course, at that time, are a substantial number of parole successes in the same community. The decision to grant parole involves the taking of calculated risks and this should be more widely appreciated. Like probation, the success of parole requires public understanding and support.
I am very interested in that aspect of this question and I urge that the minister's department do all it can to enlist the sympathetic support and understanding of representative groups in Canada. I suggest that women's organizations would be very interested in the work of helping to develop a public understanding of this type of legislation. To that end I suggest there should be some sort of pamphlet or news release or at least some sort of information given by the

minister's department to the public and, certainly, to certain representative organizations bringing to their attention the principles involved in this legislation and giving them some education as to the administration of the act, and seeking public co-operation.

subtopic: REPEAL OF TICKET OF LEAVE ACT, ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a remark or two to make on this subject, and without reiterating what others have said, may I say I was pleased to see that legislative effect is to be given to the report of the Fauteux committee. I know the committee also made recommendations with respect to other matters under the jurisdiction of the minister in one way or another which are connected with the question of parole, and we hope that those things will be given an equal amount of consideration and will lead to a type of approach similar to that expressed in this bill.
There is one important factor arising out of the bill, and that is the selection of members to constitute the parole authority or the parole board. I know the minister himself would be the first to say that the attitudes, the education background and the philosophy of these individuals must be given paramount consideration, for certainly the parole authority could make or break what is an excellent piece of legislation.
There is one recommendation which the Fauteux committee made which I have not been able to come across in the bill, and I must add that I have not had a great deal of time to look into it and compare it with the report. That was the authority of the parole board to consider, in the first instance, the legality of a particular sentence and to make a comment, if they consider that the sentence was illegal, to the attorney general of a particular province. This matter may be dealt with in the regulations which are to be made following the passage of this bill. Another is adequate preliminary studies and interviews by the board before the normal time that a person might be eligible for a parole.
There are one or two other matters that were dealt with by the Fauteux committee which have been in effect for some time, having to do with the rules with respect to considering whether an inmate in an institution should receive parole or not, and apparently one of the restrictions is that inmates who are in penal institutions because of infractions of the drugs act are not eligible for parole. I hope that the minister, when his ideas and plans for a new approach to the problem of drug addiction and the rehabilitation of addicts are in effect, will also give consideration to relaxing the rigidity of this rule which provides that no parole may be
National Parole Board
given to these people. If there is to be some scheme for the rehabilitation of drug addicts they should be allowed the same privileges as other inmates are allowed with respect to parole. Other factors may, of course, affect this situation such as people being habitual criminals or having committed other offences in connection with the offence of possessing drugs.
Another very important part of the parole system is that which follows after the parole is granted, or after a person is released on parole, and that is rehabilitative care-the supervision that has to take place after an inmate is released in order that everything possible may be done to ensure that an individual may take a better place in society and make a better contribution to society and not fall back into the ways he followed before he was placed in prison.
These are two or three thoughts, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the minister will take cognizance of them. Possibly further provision is going to be made in the regulations, and I think that if they are, that will be fine and dandy. I hope that after its passage through here and the other place it will not be long before the bill actually becomes law, and that this new system, this new approach with respect to granting parole, may come speedily into effect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF TICKET OF LEAVE ACT, ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add just a few words to this discussion as we do not want to prolong it. One of the problems we have come across with regard to parole-and I am happy it is called that now, rather than "ticket of leave" because that may be more in keeping with what we want to accomplish with regard to getting people back into normal society than "ticket of leave" would indicate-one of the problems the federal parliament is going to have to face is the ununiformity of sentences for particular offences.
We probably all know of cases where an armed bank robbery netted the accused 20 years, though in another case very similar, with a different judge and a different court, the same prisoner would have received probably four or five years. I think that one of the considerations which must be taken into consideration is this matter of sentences. There is no uniformity in sentences and that, probably, is as it should be, because we do not recommend that an armed bank robber should have a penalty of 20 years and that one where the accused is not armed should be good for five years or something like that. However, this must be taken into account in granting a parole.

National Parole Board
It has been an almost definite rule in the past that half the sentence has to be served and this is not necessarily in keeping with the nature of the crime. Uniformity must be established with respect to penalties and extenuating circumstances must be taken into consideration. It would be well for the parole board to give more consideration to the record of the individual while in prison, his home environment, the kind of family he has and circumstances of that nature rather than considering only the length of sentence first granted. Grave consideration should also be given to the regional problems that develop with respect to sentencing prisoners. We all know if there are 15 robberies in a locality-*

subtopic: REPEAL OF TICKET OF LEAVE ACT, ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
I referred to it, Mr. Speaker, only to indicate that in the past the parole was related to the sentence and the sentences had no degree of uniformity.
There are some archaic provisions attached to tickets of leave to which some consideration should be given. A parolee or person on ticket of leave is told he cannot drink alcoholic beverages, enter public houses or associate with women of easy virtue. A number of conditions they are asked to observe are not really conducive to rehabilitation. I urge that some thought be given to changing the archaic language of the regulations under which these people operate when on ticket of leave.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) a few weeks ago in the house referred to a particular appeal. With respect to parolees or people on tickets of leave there is a tendency to expect nothing good from them and the vilest rumour about them is accepted as a fact. This attitude and malicious gossip frequently results in the reincarceration of the individual and before he is recommitted he should be given the right of an appeal or hearing before a magistrate. I am not convinced that the Minister of Justice would want recommitted prisoners to serve the full length of their original sentences. After all, the purpose of penal institutions should be to equip people to return to a useful, constructive life in society. The present method of recommitting prisoners militates against the accomplishment of that constructive end.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry I missed that. Perhaps I should have mentioned it in connection with clause 12. Recommittal will generally take place under one of two circumstances; first, on conviction for an indictable offence, where parole will be automatically revoked and the parolee will then, of course, have to undergo imprisonment in connection with the new sentence as well as being liable to serve the rest of the sentence for which he was on parole. I do not imagine that my hon. friend had that in mind when he spoke of appeal or review. Probably what he had in mind was the second circumstance under which the man will go back to the institution, and that is where there has been a suspension where, by reason of some activity not amounting to the commission of an indictable offence, but perhaps amounting to a breach of the condition on which he was under parole, a report is received and
National Parole Board
recommendation made that parole be forfeited. In that case he may also be recommitted. In every such case, on receipt of a report, the parole will be suspended pending an investigation, and the board will then automatically undertake a review to see whether the suspension is justified and the parole in fact should be forfeited or whether on the other hand the suspension is not justified and the parole should be reinstituted. So that, in that type of case it is provided now that there shall always be a review by the board before there is a recommittal to the penal institution itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF TICKET OF LEAVE ACT, ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext: Take the case of an individual who is on parole after being sentenced to a 5-year term. He is out for say two and one-half years and he is recommitted for the number of things that are in the present ticket of leave requirement, namely that he cannot associate with certain people, he cannot do certain things. Would he still be required to serve the five years that he originally received?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPEAL OF TICKET OF LEAVE ACT, ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD, ETC.
speechtext:
No, he would not be liable
in any case to serve more than that portion of the sentence which remained unexpired at the time he was released on parole. One of the objects of recommittal in such a case would be to prevent the man from committing a further crime, or an indictable offence, to give him, as it were, a fresh chance for parole. The theory is that it is preferable to get him back in time to prevent him from actually committing the new offence, back into an institution where the reformation and rehabilitation program and training may be recommenced with a view toward a further release on parole. So the mere fact that he has been recommitted in such a case does not necessarily mean that he has to serve the full remainder of the unexpired portion of his sentence. That is the maximum that he can serve; but it is quite possible, and indeed it would be the desire of the parole authorities and the prison authorities-to recommence the training and rehabilitation program so that he might, if possible, be released on parole again before the expiration of the full sentence.
