speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minisier of Transport) moved
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Railway Act to permit certain grants to be made from the railway grade crossing fund; to credit to the railway grade crossing fund in each fiscal year the sum of $5 million to aid actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of crossings; and for certain changes in connection with the administration of the fund.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that hon. members will wish me to indicate briefly and in a general way what is being proposed in the legislation that will be introduced following the adoption of this resolution.
As hon. members know, there is a fund known as the railway grade crossing fund from which contributions are made to assist work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of railway-highway crossings. Section 265 of the Railway

Act sets forth the work toward which contributions will be made and the maximum amounts that may be contributed to each project.
One of the purposes of the proposed legislation is to increase, during a period of three years, the maximum contributions that may be made from the fund. The main estimates of the Department of Transport for this fiscal year contain a credit of $10 million to the fund in addition to the normal annual credit of $5 million. It is the intention of the government to provide a similar additional sum of $10 million next year and the following year. These additional credits and the proposed increases in the permissible contributions will, I am confident, serve a double purpose of encouraging the initiation of additional projects to make crossings safer and affording a greater measure of financial assistance than is now available to municipalities and other parties who have to bear the cost of such work.
The present maximum contribution from the fund towards work in respect of a crossing at rail level is 60 per cent of the cost of the work or $300,000, whichever is the lesser. The proposed legislation, and I trust that hon. members will permit me to mention some details, would increase for three years the 60 per cent to 80 per cent and the $300,000 to $500,000. These contributions are available towards automatic protection at level crossings and also, for example, where a grade separation is ordered to eliminate an existing level crossing.
In the case of reconstruction and improvement of existing grade separations, such as a dangerous subway, the present maximum contribution is 30 per cent or $150,000, whichever is the lesser. The amendment will increase the 30 per cent to 50 per cent and the $150,000 to $250,000.
Provision will also be made to permit contributions towards the cost of placing reflective markings on the sides of railways cars. Such markings serve to warn motorists when a train is at a crossing which they are approaching at night.
There is also an amendment to subsection 5 of section 265 to ensure that there will be statutory annual credit of $5 million to the fund. There is a limitation in the present subsection which makes it possible for the annual credit to be less than $5 million if at the start of the fiscal year there happens to be more than $2 million uncommitted in the fund at that time. This limitation is being removed. This, of course, is a statutory annual credit and, as I have already stated, it is being supplemented by an additional $10 million this year and will also be so supplemented in each of the next two years.

Another provision will give the board of transport commissioners power to order that the words "railway crossing" on level crossing signboards be made reflective at crossings where the board so orders. The present section 270 of the Railway Act requires that the words be only painted on the signboards.
The legislation is comparatively brief and I have outlined its principal provisions. I may add that when the bill is given second reading it is my intention to move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the legislation announced by the minister in introducing the resolution is of extreme importance not only to parliament but I am sure to all those who are interested in this problem. At first blush the legislation is not only welcomed by this side of the house but will receive our support as it is discussed in its various stages, subject, of course, to any constructive criticism we may have to make as we go along.
As I read the resolution which the minister has brought before the house it is divided into three parts. The first is that a measure should be introduced to amend the Railway Act to permit certain grants to be made from the railway grade crossing fund. The second is to credit to the railway grade crossing fund in each fiscal year the sum of $5 million to aid actual construction work for protection at crossings. The third is to cover certain changes in connection with the administration of the fund, as the minister has explained in greater detail in his submission to the house.
Before I go on with my main remarks I should like to say that I have some difficulty in understanding the second portion of the resolution, namely, that crediting to the railway grade crossing fund in each fiscal year the sum of $5 million. That has already been done, as I understand it and as I will explain later, by the amendment to the Railway Act passed in 1955 found in 3-4 Elizabeth II, chapter 41. I will come back to that in a moment.
At this stage I should like to say that this problem was of such importance that the former administration determined to ask the board of transport commissioners to make a very careful study and investigation of the whole grade crossing problem. An order in council was passed on January 14, 1953 covering the investigation to which I have referred, an investigation was to be made into all phases of the problem of railway-highway crossings under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
In order not to labour the matter unduly but so that the committee may gather an idea 57071-3-237
Railway Act
of what the then administration had in mind, perhaps I may be allowed to put on the record the governing parts of the order in council. The board was asked to do three things, first, conduct a survey and report upon methods considered by the board to be practicable, under all pertinent circumstances, to eliminate the hazards and improve the public convenience and the protection and safety of the public at such crossings; second, review and report on the adequacy of the railway grade crossing fund to provide for the construction of works for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of railway-highway crossings; and, finally, to make such recommendations as the board might deem advisable in the premises.
I hold in my hand the report made by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada on May 10, 1954 containing a review of the hearings that the board held from one end of the country to the other and a detailed statement of its recommendations. Any one who is interested in the problem of railway grade crossings and the railway grade crossing fund will find in this document interesting reading covering all phases of the problem. The board sat for many months. This investigation was the first of its kind undertaken since the creation of the railway grade crossing fund in 1909 and the board gathered a great volume of data and statistics over a period of 12 months.
I should like to state briefly now what the recommendations were that the board made to the government on May 10, 1954, because they lead up to the discussion now before the house. The recommendations made by the board were eight in number.
The first of these was that an appropriation of $5 million instead of the then $1 million, which was payable into the fund, be made beginning April 1 in any such year. The second was that the contribution provided out of the grade crossing fund be increased from 40 per cent to 60 per cent, with a maximum of $150,000 in respect of any one crossing at rail levels. The third had to do with construction and improvement of grade operations in existence and recommended that the contribution in any one case should not exceed 30 per cent of the cost of reconstruction and improvement, nor exceed $150,000. The fourth, which is interesting and about which I shall have something to say at a later period, states that a contribution should be directed towards the annual cost of maintenance and operation of automatic signals installed at crossings after this amendment recommended goes into force, and that the contribution in respect of any one crossing shall not exceed in any year the actual cost for that year.

Railway Act
should be an advisory committee representing the railways, the provinces, the municipalities and the board of transport commissioners. I believe that such an advisory committee should meet once a year or twice a year, if need be, to consider all the applications across Canada, including all the applications coming from the provinces. To me this would be an excellent thing because here would be construction projects which could be used for all-year employment and particularly for winter employment. The consideration of that proposal is to be found in the report. I believe it is worth studying.
Then I recommend that there be established a sub-committee of the board of transport commissioners to deal with these cases. Here again, I am not suggesting in any way that the board of transport commissioners cannot deal effectively, as it is now constituted, with the applications that come before it. What I am saying is that the board of transport commissioners in this day and age has very many other responsibilities having to do with freight rates, pipe lines, water rates and many other important activities. So it would seem to me that the board would be well advised to set up a subcommittee of itself composed of three members or even fewer to go about the country and deal with the applications as rapidly and effectively as may be.
Finally, it seems to me that there should be greater co-ordination between the parties interested in this problem. After all, instead of three parties concerned getting away from each other it seems to me that they should be brought closer and closer together. This is not exclusively a federal problem. Because of the constitution it falls also within the jurisdiction of the provinces and the municipalities, and since this matter is becoming more and more acute it seems to me that the parties should be co-ordinated and brought closer together by means of consultations once a year, twice a year or even more often so that the problem might be dealt with more efficiently and so that the protection which all of us want can be given to the public faster as the applications develop.
These are the five suggestions which I make to the minister, and I am sure he will realize at once that they are not made in any destructive manner but for the sole purpose of being helpful with reference to this allimportant problem. I do not want to resume my seat without pointing out to the committee that this is not the first time that the problem has received the attention of the government. I cannot remember one occasion during the nine years when I sat on the other side of the house as the minister of transport

when it did not occupy a great deal of the time of hon. members, either by way of discussion on the estimates or by way of discussion under the legislation which was brought down from time to time. The most comprehensive and the best report on this whole question is, as I said, to be found in the report on the railroad-highway crossing problem in Canada which was published on May 10, 1954, pursuant to an order in council.
To the extent that this resolution and the bill which will follow will not only implement the recommendations contained in that report and will go beyond the legislation brought down by my predecessor, it is welcome, and I can assure the minister and the house that it will receive the wholehearted support of the members who sit on this side.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a moment before six o'clock to congratulate the minister on this legislation which will be of such obvious advantage to the constituency which I represent.
I should like to refer just for a moment to another aspect of this announced legislation which concerns the marking of the freight cars to which the minister referred in his opening remarks. This is a matter which has come to my attention over the years from a number of sources and from no source better qualified than Bert Long of the Willowdale Enterprise who for some years through his editorial columns has urged some action in this regard.
I wish again to congratulate the minister for the progressive step he has taken in the direction of marking freight cars adequately so as to prevent the recurrence of so many accidents which have occurred at level crossings at night.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in this group welcome the proposed amendments to the Railway Act particularly in view of the fact that the increased number of cars on the highways today has made the incidence of accidents much higher. It has been reported that in 1909 there were less than 5,000 automobiles in Canada and in 1958 there are approximately four million motor vehicles on our highways. This indicates something of the scope of the problem concerning grade crossings many of which are in rural areas.

I have a personal interest in the present amendments because it was only four years ago that my uncle, aunt and four of their children met their death when the motor vehicle in which they were travelling struck a diesel engine as they were driving to church one Sunday morning. I am sure all hon. members know of accidents that have occurred at crossings where no accident should have occurred. My aunt and uncle were survived by several children who even today suffer as a result of the untimely death of their parents. My uncle had lived in the area where the accident occurred all his life and had frequently travelled the road and passed the crossing. He knew exactly when the trains came and could anticipate their time of arrival. The visibility was not too good on the day of the accident and my uncle's car and the diesel engine arrived at the crossing simultaneously. Here was a person who knew the area well and was familiar with the schedules of the trains. He was a cautious driver, was always on the lookout for trains and it was reported that he was driving at a speed of 20 miles an hour at the time of the accident. This type of thing leads one to wonder how accidents of this kind can occur.
I am pleased to welcome the amendments to the act which will assist in meeting the problem. The railway with which we are concerned in my area is the Ontario Northland railway. We discussed the accident with the commissioners and made several recommendations to them. It was pointed out that when the railways switched from the use of steam engines to diesel engines the latter had a different sounding whistle. The warning whistle on steam engines could be heard for a considerable distance but it has been borne out by investigations that the warning whistle on diesel engines tends to funnel the sound forward and it is not heard to any extent on either side. We recommended the adoption of whistles like those used on steam engines with which people are familiar and which are loud enough to provide adequate warning of the approaching engine.
Another recommendation that was made was that strips of Scotch light tape be used at the front of engines and cars and along the sides and I am pleased to observe that a provision to this effect is included in the amendments before us.
The solution to the number of motor accidents at grade crossings will not be entirely met by the construction of over-passes and under-passes because many people and particularly young men have been killed on them. These appear to exert a fascination over youths. When going through an underpass in an old car the exhaust makes a lusty noise
Railway Act
which I suppose encourages the young drivers to travel faster. There is also the danger created by snow, ice and sleet conditions particularly in under-passes. I am convinced that no one solution will be arrived at to meet the problem. One measure that would contribute to safety at crossings would be the erection of signs bearing print outlined with Scotch light tape similar to that used on highway signs. It is visible at night and more effective than the cross-arm signs the railways now use. This could be adapted for railway use and I am sure it would result in saving many lives.
We cannot emphasize too strongly the need for improving grade crossings. One night last winter during the election campaign I was travelling in a rural area with which I am not completely familiar. I had taken a shortcut and as I drove along the side road I was startled to see the headlight of an approaching train a few hundred feet down the track. Prior to that moment I had not been aware of a railway crossing because I had seen no signs. Any moneys spent in improving the safety at railway crossings are spent for the benefit of all Canadians and the minister is to be congratulated for the amendments he is now introducing.
It must be borne in mind that it is easier for the federal government to pay its share of projects of this kind than it is for the municipal and provincial governments to pay their shares.
Speaking in this house on April 18, 1955, when the Railway Act was being revised the present Minister of Finance cited some figures which I believe should be placed on the record again. After speaking of the number of accidents that occurred at crossings and outlining the need for increased protection the hon. member said, as reported at page 2905 of Hansard of that date:
What has been the contribution to the solution of this problem by various types of crossing protection? A further glance at these figures indicates that over three-quarters of these accidents which have occurred at public highway crossings on railways have occurred at unprotected crossings.
Later in the same debate he said:
Then in the case of accidents that took the form of motor vehicles running into the side of trains- and there are many of these accidents-last year there were 140 of them, of which 46 occurred in daylight hours and 94 during the night hours.
The provision in the amendments before us for illuminating the fronts and sides of engines and of boxcars with fluorescent tape will eliminate to some extent the large preponderance of accidents that occur after dark. A friend of mine was driving along a road in Porcupine a year or so ago under bad conditions. There was a slight amount of

Railway Act
rain and some fog. Although he knew the area quite well visibility was bad and he was driving at dusk. He drove into the side of a slow-moving freight train and broke his leg and sustained other injuries. In this particular case if there had been any kind of warning on the sides of the box cars this accident would not have happened because he would have been able to see the train long before he did. Further development is necessary to protect the Canadian public on open railway crossings.
I would ask the minister to give some consideration to the matter of changing the type of horns the diesels use because I know myself that it was much easier to hear the old steam whistle than it is to hear the modern diesel whistles. I am also aware of the fact that the government of Ontario has done some development work in this field. They realize the problem but to date they have not seen fit to complete the development so that it can be made available to the industry. I would ask the minister to give some attention to that form of protection.

Mr. Chairman, the matter of railway grade level crossings is one in which I have taken an active part for the last four or five years. The question has been before the house continuously. It goes back to the beginning of the century and the cry that we have always heard is that the work was not being accomplished fast enough and sufficient funds were not appropriated to cover the situation. In fact, we have been told that the problem of grade level crossings was getting beyond the power of the board of transport commissioners to cope with because of cost. The last time the figure was given it was in the neighbourhood of 33,000 grade level crossings of one kind or another. In the neighbourhood of 2,000 to 2,500 were classified as grade separations.
During the last three years a request came from all sides of the house, irrespective of party, that the amount of $1 million a year which was appropriated to take care of the situation should be increased. It was also said that the decrease in the percentages that the board of transport commissioners required the municipalities and the railways to pay was even beyond their ability. An appeal was made that the matter be looked into again and that the board of transport commissioners undertake a review of the situation. In 1954 the board brought down a very comprehensive report. They covered the problem very well, but the sum and substance of their report was that the problem was of such magnitude that it was practically beyond the capacity of the government to solve the problem.

At that time we appealed to the government for an increase in the funds and the government increased the contribution to the fund from $1 million to $5 million. They increased the percentage which the board of transport commissioners would pay to 60 per cent, 25 per cent by the municipalities and 15 per cent by the railways. But that was also too low. At that time we asked the government to increase the amount to $15 million and also increase the percentage that the board of transport commissioners should pay to relieve the municipalities and the railways themselves of as much of the burden as possible. As I said, we asked for $15 million. Of course, the government of the day could not see its way clear to appropriate that amount, but this government in its wisdom increased it last year to $15 million for the time being on a make-work basis. I am pleased to hear that they have also increased the maximum amount that the board should pay, but it has not yet been determined what the railways or the municipalities will be asked to contribute. I appeal to the minister to make representations to the government for a larger amount.
If hon. members take the trouble to read the 1954 report of the board they will see that they outlined a hypothetical program that would cost $30 million a year. Spread over 25 years it would amount to $750 million to inaugurate a program from coast to coast which would attempt to do something about this problem which is causing great concern to the people of Canada. But after stating that, the sum and substance of the report was that it would take care of only some 1,400 grade level separations of a major nature. Grade separated crossings generally cost from $1 million to $2,350,000. Inflation has raised that cost to a greater amount. These are the crossings where the most accidents happen.
The hon. member mentioned the rate of accidents. I do not think the percentage has changed to any great extent. Every three days two people are killed somewhere in Canada on grade level crossings. About a year ago the government did inaugurate a program that was started by what was called a national safety council, which is similar to the Ontario safety league. This was to be a national safety league. The president of the Shell Oil Company was the chairman. He succeeded Mr. Claxton, who was at one time minister of national defence. Mr. Claxton took charge in the first year and then he was succeeded by Mr. Ash of the Shell Oil Company. They were to inaugurate a safety system throughout the Dominion of Canada to try to co-ordinate safety regulations from

one end of Canada to the other and endeavour to keep them uniform. Signs at the crossings were to be put far enough from the crossings to give sufficient warning to motorists. The difficulty was that they ran into trouble with the municipalities with respect to the maintenance of those signs and for permission to encroach and the responsibility for enforcement. These are the things that came up in the discussion about grade level crossings the last three or four years.
I would suggest to the government that they give careful consideration to the hypothetical program outlined by the board of transport commissioners and consider it carefully on a make-work basis, particularly when unemployment is prevalent.
The board of transport commissioners have plans for grade separations. They take a long time to construct and they cost plenty but a start should soon be made on them. The sum of $30 million a year would be a great help and it would spark the program to make work in Canada at this time. As the situation is today we are not keeping up with the number of new grade level crossings created throughout the year. This program would not only reduce the hazards of grade level crossings but it would also serve the purpose of making work. I would certainly suggest that the minister take another look at it to see if he cannot increase the amount put into the fund and also go into the situation more thoroughly because the railways are in the position where they cannot pay. The municipalities are finding it almost impossible to meet the burden of cost and they cannot raise any more money by taxes. Probably, in the circumstances, and for an interim period, the government should take on the whole cost of constructing grade level crossings and try to solve the problem and this is the only way it can be done.
I could give details on how many grade level crossings need to be protected, how many wig-wags there are, the number of people being killed, and so on. The fact is that the situation is getting beyond us and the board of transport commissioners admits that is so. They claim that $30 million a year would only begin to scratch the surface. Therefore, if the government would reconsider the percentage basis on which the municipalities and railways have to contribute and allot more money to take care of the problem I know this would be a progressive improvement. Before the resolution carries I should like to ask the minister when the municipalities and railways will be able to take advantage of the new arrangements under this legislation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND APPLICATION AND INCREASE AMOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this resolution was under discussion last Monday I was saying something about the problems some of the mines have and I was pointing out that the subsidization of the Hollinger mine, for instance, amounted to something over half a million dollars and they paid a dividend on a profit of something over a million dollars. The payment of that subsidy has certainly had some effect on the profits that particular mine has been able to make
3740	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold. Mining Assistance Act in the last few years. While that subsidy has been advantageous for Hollinger, on the other hand the largest gold mine on this continent, Kerr-Addison in the Larder Lake group, has never been able to qualify at any time for emergency gold mining assistance. They still sell their gold on the open market and therefore if any impetus is going to be given to that particular mine it has to be done in a different manner.
This problem has been discussed at great length by numerous people. In the past commissioners have been set up by provincial and federal governments to discuss the problems of the gold mining industry. A number of suggestions have been made and it is accepted that the problem is one concerning which the federal government is going to have to do something. In "A Social Approach to Economics" published in 1939, pages 506 and 507, Professors H. A. Logan and M. K. Inman have pointed out that the economic philosophy of our society has accepted the concept that every commodity should sell for enough to cover all of its legitimate costs in its price.
In the case of gold, if prices are not sufficient to cover the cost of producing the quantities of gold which our country may require, there are two alternative public policies which can be adopted. The first one is to raise the price of gold. This, however, the nation cannot do independently of other nations. I suggest that it can be done if the government will make the necessary changes so that it can buy gold and store it in the same way that the United States does. If we raised the price of gold to $45 or $50 an ounce or even $70 an ounce, as suggested by some in the gold mining industry, this would have a great influence on the amount of money that would be available in Canada and the expansion that could take place because of the gold being held in reserve in this country. It would also be advantageous to mines like Kerr-Addison that have not been able to receive any federal subsidy.
The second policy is for the nation to absorb or reduce some of the production costs of the marginal firms in the industry through various forms of subsidization. This the nation has done through cost-aid grants, taxation concessions and in other ways. Cost-aid grants have gone largely to firms operating at a cost well below the $35 margin. They have resulted in lower employment, wages and output than would have been obtained if the same amount of subsidies had been distributed directly to labour. In the case of the mines in the Porcupine camp, the 1951-52 cost-aid grants were equivalent to about $450 per year per worker. You can see that the increase of 25 per cent now being made will amount to less than $150 and thus it can be seen that


even if all this money were given to these particular mines the situation would not be a great deal different from what it has been.
Looking at the situation on a long term basis, I think that the first thing that will have to be done is to remove the word "emergency" from the federal government's cost-aid program. Conditions have not changed for the better in the years that the legislation has been in force but have worsened. The costs of all requirements of the mines have risen rapidly while at the same time the price of the product has been pegged at the world market price, with the mines at times receiving less than that amount because of the premium on the Canadian dollar. Therefore we are going to have to continue this form of subsidy on a long term basis.
Second and more important, I think we have to give more consideration to the establishment of new secondary industries in northern Ontario. We are going to have to have diversification of industries. In my opinion the federal government has an obligation to see that the towns of Timmins, Kirkland Lake and Larder Lake do not disappear even when there is no more gold. When speaking the other day on the northern affairs estimates I suggested that the problem probably could be solved in part by the establishment of a new trade route through northern Ontario and James bay and Hudson bay as an alternative to the St. Lawrence seaway. Such a long term program will need assistance and I think that the government could quite easily divert a percentage of the assistance it is now giving under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act toward developing this new trade route. Secondly, some of this aid that we are now giving to the gold mines could be advanced to other industries.
There are a number of other things, in addition to the emergency gold mining assistance, which are done for the gold mining industry. When a new mine comes into production, it pays no taxes for the first three years. If we were willing to extend that type of concession to secondary industries it would provide an inducement for them to come into northern Ontario. We also have a railway there, and I am quite sure that consideration could be given to an inducement to secondary industries in the form of lower freight rates on certain commodities that they use.
This problem has become apparent not only to the chambers of commerce, the miners who work in these areas, the citizens of the area, but it has become apparent to the municipalities. I referred to this booklet entitled "The Gold Mining Community", published by the municipalities. I should like, in closing, to read the last paragraph in which reference

is made to this need for secondary industries, as well as the need for a long term program so that development will move forward rather than become stagnant waiting for the mines to die or get a little better price for their products. They point out what it takes to start a secondary industry and the basic requirements needed for the development of secondary industries as well as some of the problems we have in northern Ontario in that regard. They end up with this statement:
The drive for economic diversification is strong in the gold mining communities, whose residents and leaders are well aware of their position. What is required is something more than hard work, optimistic talk, and detailed planning. That something consists essentially of potential markets, for without them productive potential means nothing. The southern front of progress comes to mind first. But if the northland is to rescue the gold mining communities, they will have to survive until northern promise comes to fruition. As in the case of underwriting gold, then, the subsidizing of economic diversification is essentially a play for time.
I would suggest to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys that he could do a great deal for the communities of northern Ontario that are now totally dependent upon gold mining if he would give consideration to some of the requests that these municipalities have made. He, first, should remove the word "emergency" from the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, and make it the gold mining assistance act so the mines would know this assistance would be continued year after year. Secondly, he should have an amendment written into this act that would require the mines, when they receive this subsidy, to turn at least part of it over to the miners in the form of higher wages, a pension plan and better fringe benefits. The municipalities have now realized, for the first time, in the presentation of this brief, that the miners themselves are the people who keep the mining communities alive. If the miner gets more money he will spend it in the community, and that will result in better conditions for everybody. If mines like the Hollinger are to turn this subsidy over to their coupon clippers, many of whom do not even live in Canada, then these mining areas are not going to receive much benefit from this legislation.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Mr. Chairman, I heard the minister's argument and I cannot see how his argument is a valid one. After all, the federal government is paying a great deal of money to Canadian enterprise or to other levels of government and is attaching conditions to such payments. I fail to see why in this case the government cannot, in agreeing to increase the subsidy by 25 per cent, attach a condition to such payment. For example, the federal government will pay a portion of the cost of a bridge on the trans-Canada highway provided the bridge is a toll-free

bridge. There is a condition there which the provincial government is obliged to meet. Even in the payment of the subsidy itself, the mines must meet certain conditions.
I fail to see why one of those conditions could not well be that part of this federal subsidy be payable to the employees; that a company must be able to convince the minister that the employees concerned have shared in the benefits or will share in the benefits; and that unless the company concerned is able to satisfy the minister that the workers actually will share in this subsidy then the subsidy shall not be payable in such cases. I believe that if the government wanted to do so it could easily insert such a condition for the payment of the subsidy.
After all, we are not primarily concerned with the welfare of the companies. We are taking this money from the taxpayers of this country. The taxpayers are paying this money in order to keep the employees employed and they would like to see these employees employed at normal wage rates. The minister knows full well that those wage rates for that type of mining in these gold mining communities are not normal; they are less than normal. The favourite complaint for many long years now-and I have heard the complaint for five years now-has been that these companies have not shared the subsidy with their workers that they have taken the subsidy and have regarded it as their own and that thus the intent of the subsidy has been lost in a goodly number of cases.
The letter read by the minister from the town of Timmins expresses, of course, the attitude that all of us have. We are glad that assistance is being given. However, that letter has nothing whatsoever to do with the request that was made the other day by the hon. member for Timmins and is now being repeated by the hon. member for Timis-kaming. I know of people who have gone into those stopes that are closed year after year and have taken one carload or two carloads of muck out-four or five tons, ten tons at most -so as to build up their millheads to bring the price of the product up to where they want to keep it. These mines have ores which could have been mined a long time ago, but the companies are not mining them because they have been living on this subsidy. If the government continues this type of assistance the moneys are only going into the pockets of the shareholders and are doing very little to keep these communities alive.

Broadcasting

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue) moved
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to establish a board of broadcast governors to regulate broadcasting in Canada; to provide that the expenditure of the board shall be paid out of money appropriated by parliament therefor and also to provide for the continuance of a corporation known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the purpose of operating a national broadcasting service in Canada; and to provide further for the payment, remuneration, salaries and fees of the officers and employees thereof.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry? Carried. Shall I report the resolution?

I would be very happy, Mr. Chairman, if the committee would accept your suggestion that this resolution carry, then I would dispense with any remarks I might make. I shall speak for a few minutes on this since it is one of the most important matters with which the Canadian public and this parliament are concerned. I think perhaps the committee will expect me to say a few words on the resolution itself. I have spoken, as some hon. members recall, in this committee on two occasions this session on the matter of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself and broadcasting generally. I certainly do not intend to repeat tonight anything I might have said on those occasions.
I want to refer specifically to the resolution which is before the committee. This party, of which the government is now constituted, in days past has urged that there should be a Canadian regulatory body which would be in control of broadcasting in this country, both privately owned and publicly owned. Hon. members know that up to the present time the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the publicly owned corporation, has exercised this regulatory function over the whole industry as well as acting as operator of the publicly owned system. In order to determine this issue and many others concerning broadcasting, the preceding government in 1955 appointed a royal commission to study and report upon the problems of broadcasting. I think it was December 2, 1955, that the order in council was passed appointing a royal commission. This royal commission reported on March 15, 1957, but because of divers and sundry events, which are well known to all members of this house, interruptions took place and there was no particular time in which this matter could be considered up until now.
[Mr. Comtois.l
This commission was headed by Mr. Robert Fowler of Montreal, and the report, which is well known I think to all hon. members, is popularly called the Fowler report. Other members of the commission were Mr. Edmond Turcotte, who at that time was our ambassador to Colombia, and the third member was Mr. Stewart, who at that time was president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and is now chairman of the board. The commission spent a great deal of time in studying this matter, travelled across Canada and had many hearings, and although their views in the report may not be acceptable to all, and perhaps the report as a whole could not be accepted by any one person, yet I think whatever may be said about the report itself, it is certainly one of the most interestingly written reports that has ever been written by any royal commission. If hon. members have not read it, I think they will find the reading of it will repay them, both because of the content and because of the style in which the report is written.
I stated the position which some of us had taken in the past with respect to regulation, and I should like for a minute or two to refer to the report to see what it had to say because it deals specifically with the resolution before us. On page 90 of the royal commission report, we find this:
We think there have in fact been two public elements involved in radio and television broadcasting. This factual separation of powers should be more precisely defined in law. One of these elements should be an operating agency, engaged in the operation of publicly owned stations and national networks and in the production and distribution of a national program service throughout Canada.
Then, on page 91, the report says:
The other public agency in the Canadian broadcasting field should be a board created and authorized to act for parliament, and responsible to parliament, for the direction and supervision of the Canadian broadcasting system. This board should have responsibility for all elements in Canadian broadcasting. It should not, we suggest, be part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its members should not, as in the present statute, comprise the corporation.
Then, farther along on that same page we find this:
This board is not part of the C.B.C. and should not be referred to as "the board of governors of C.B.C." We suggest that a new board, differently named, should be created by statute. The name we use in speaking of this agency is "the board of broadcast governors".
If hon. members look at the resolution before them, they will find that the first clause says:
-it is expedient to establish a board of broadcast governors to regulate broadcasting in Canada;

This is the name recommended by the royal commission and the object also was suggested by the royal commission.
The second part of the resolution provides for the continuance of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am told that in some quarters at some time there were some fears and some doubts expressed as to the attitude that this government might take towards the publicly owned broadcasting system in Canada. If these fears were expressed at any time, Mr. Chairman, I am sure they have been dissipated before this. The other day that distinguished Canadian scholar and historian, Dr. Creighton, headed a very large delegation which appeared before the Prime Minister and myself in connection with this problem of broadcasting. I think some of the words used by him on that occasion could well be reproduced in Hansard. Speaking of broadcasting in Canada, Dr. Creighton said:
Canadian strength and Canadian unity ultimately depend upon Canada's maintenance of her autonomy and spiritual independence on the North American continent. Throughout our history we have persistently followed national policies devised to strengthen our unity from ocean to ocean and to maintain our separateness in North America. Our defences against the "continentalism", which has so often threatened us from the south, have been based on the east-west axis provided by nature, the strong line of the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes and the Saskatchewan. Confederation gave us our transcontinental political union. Sir John Macdonald's national policy provided the framework for an integrated transcontinental economy. A national broadcasting system can do for us, in the realm of the mind and the spirit, precisely what these old and tested national policies have done in the political and economic sphere. A steady flow of live programs along the east-west lifeline will express Canadian ideas and ideals, employ Canadian talent, and help unite our people from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that represents the views of this government with respect to the functions, maintenance and strengthening of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Provision is made for this in the second clause of the resolution which is before you, of course with the concomitant factors of the provision of funds by parliament for this purpose. It is not necessary for me to speak longer on this matter at the moment. Obviously, the removing of the regulatory powers from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and providing a separate board have created certain administrative difficulties and certain problems in connection with the drafting of this legislation which could be dealt with much better when the bill is before the house. I trust, Mr. Chairman, that the committee will see fit to pass this resolution at as early a date as possible, so that the bill can be brought down and the details of the legislation considered by hon. members. Then, on
Broadcasting
second reading, the whole matter can be given careful and full consideration.

I think the minister can be assured, Mr. Chairman, that the hope he has just expressed will be realized, namely, that the committee will pass this resolution as soon as it sees fit. This is a very important resolution, as the minister has pointed out, dealing with a very important subject. I think it does require discussion, although I agree that perhaps that discussion can be focused more directly on the problem of broadcasting when we have the bill before us. Nevertheless, it is such an important matter, as the minister has indicated, that some observations even on the resolution are required.
My first reaction to the introduction of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, is that it is unfortunate-for reasons which the minister perhaps knows more about than I do-whatever the reasons may be, that a resolution dealing with such a fundamental matter as this should be introduced in what we hope are the dying days of this session. Whether or not that expression will prove to be accurate, I am not sure. The house will recall that some weeks ago we moved an amendment, on going into supply which precipitated a discussion of this whole question of broadcasting; and in that amendment we expressed the hope that this matter could be dealt with early in the session. The reason for that, as the minister will understand, is obvious. This is such an important matter that it deserves careful and adequate consideration. There is nothing much more important, as the minister has pointed out on more than one occasion and even tonight, in maintaining and strengthening Canadian nationalism, pride and national identity than maintaining and strengthening a strong Canadian broadcasting system operated in the national interest.
This resolution is no doubt based on the speech from the throne or at least derives from the speech from the throne in which the government, through His Excellency the Governor General, tells us that there would be placed before the house a proposal to establish a new agency to regulate broadcasting in Canada and to ensure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the privately owned broadcasting stations work effectively together to constitute a national system to provide satisfactory television and radio services to all Canadians within reach. The speech from the throne contains the expression "to constitute a national system", an expression which is not used in this resolution. Then the paragraph in the speech from the throne goes on to say as follows: Related amendments to the Radio Act will also be proposed.

Broadcasting
I do not know what are the intentions of the the government in that regard. The last paragraph in the speech from the throne also bears on this matter because it states categorically:
You will be asked to set up a select committee on broadcasting-
Mr. Chairman, this matter is so important that I hope that the statement of the government in that respect in the speech from the throne will be carried out and that this bill, when it comes before the house, can be given first reading and then be submitted to a select committee on broadcasting for that kind of consideration which it should get, dealing as it does with a matter of such great importance. Surely legislation of this type and of this national significance should not be rushed through the house in the closing days of a session. It should go to a committee where it can get the consideration to which it is entitled.
In this connection perhaps I might be permitted to put on the record a paragraph of an editoral appearing in the Montreal Star of August 16 which expresses this idea very clearly. This paragraph reads as follows:
Granted that everything which has leaked out so far concerning the government's intentions toward broadcasting indicates a much more reasoned approach than party firebrands were hinting a few years ago. It looks as though recommendations of the Fowler commission still provide the guiding line.
We had some confirmation of that this evening. I was glad to get it.
But the select committee, which the government promised, should be allowed to study the bill before it comes up for second and third reading. For the sake of the future of broadcasting, this legislation should also be allowed to stand over.
That is the opinion of the editor of that newspaper and there is a great deal to be said for that careful, constructive course being followed in this matter. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian broadcasting system is such a complex and delicately balanced one that any changes to it, even changes which may appear to be minor, might destroy that balance, against the public interest and perhaps in favour of the private element of the system, an element which I agree is indispensable to the working of the system but which from the national point of view cannot be as important in our minds as is the public interest. I therefore suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we in this house have a duty to give this bill the most careful consideration possible, and I do not see how that can be done in the circumstances in which we find ourselves at the present time unless it is sent to a committee where it can be considered without haste, without prejudice and without partiality.

The resolution itself is before us on which a bill will be submitted; and we will have a chance, whatever happens, to examine that bill whether it goes to a committee or not, with the care which it deserves. The resolution says this:
Resolved, that it is expedient to establish a board of broadcast governors to regulate broadcasting in Canada;
In his remarks a few moments ago the minister indicated that the government intends to follow the recommendations of the Fowler commission in this respect because that is the designation given to the body recommended by the Fowler commission. He thought that this might serve to remove any fears and suspicions that we had on this side that some fundamental change with regard to the regulatory system would be introduced. If we had any such fears or anxieties as to the attitude of the government towards the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, perhaps this resolution does help to remove or to minimize those fears. But I would suggest to the minister that if we had them, they were based on statements previously made and views held by hon. members opposite on the treasury benches when they were on this side of the house. We remember some of the statements made at that time. That perhaps will explain to the minister the nature of our suspicions and our fears. That is one reason why we are scrutinizing this resolution very carefully indeed, as we will scrutinize the bill.
In this connection, the first thing that occurs to me is the wording of the first line of the resolution.
Resolved, that it is expedient to establish a board of broadcast governors to regulate broadcasting in Canada.
Normally the phraseology in a resolution of this kind-and I do not know what the significance of the omission is in this case- would be as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a board of broadcast governors to regulate broadcasting in Canada.
Indeed, in the resolution on the order paper immediately preceding the one with which we are dealing, namely item No. 18 on the order paper, that is the phraseology used.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And in item No. 17 on the order paper.

And in item No. 17 also and others. The one immediately preceding item No. 19 reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure-

And so on. Perhaps the minister will explain to us why this resolution dealing with such a very important matter omits those words "to introduce a measure".
Then the resolution goes on:
-to provide that the expenditure of the board shall be paid out of money appropriated by parliament therefor and also to provide for the continuance of a corporation known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the purpose of operating a national broadcasting service in Canada; and to provide further for the payment, remuneration, salaries and fees of the officers and employees thereof.
Note, this is not to provide for the expenses of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as such; not to provide for the money which will be needed to carry on the work of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but to provide for the payment, remuneration and salaries and fees of the officers and employees thereof. And that is all. No doubt the minister will have something to say about this. And then, of course, as I said earlier, there is nothing said in this resolution as to maintaining and strengthening the Canadian broadcasting system. We have here only a reference to a national broadcasting service, that is, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
One of the most important things in this resolution is the kind of board of broadcast governors to be set up to regulate broadcasting in Canada; how its regulations are to be made effective, and particularly what effect they will have in regard to the control of private broadcasting in this country. There could be various kinds of boards of broadcast governors, some of which we on this side would certainly not be able to support. But the kind of board of broadcast governors recommended by the Fowler commission is something else.
There are other principles in this report to which the minister has referred which we would certainly like to see included in any legislation based on this resolution. While I am not going into this matter in detail at this time I am going to outline in a very general way our position with regard to what we think should be included in any bill based on this resolution. We feel strongly-and we will make our feelings known when this bill is produced-that any legislation based on this resolution should make provision for the following things:
1.	The continued existence, with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as its operating part, as now constituted, of a single system in which both public and private stations are all integral parts and which is regulated and controlled by a single board representing the public interest.
From what the minister has said tonight and from what he has said in this house previously
Broadcasting
this session, I hope he would not quarrel with this principle and that he would perhaps see that it is embodied in the bill.
We think the legislation should also provide:
2.	Regulations to be enforced by any board of broadcast governors to ensure that the services provided by both public and private stations should meet the needs and desires of the people as a whole and not be used primarily as an industry to be exploited for commercial ends.
We accept, of course, the fact that private stations must operate in such a way as to make a profit. If they do not do that, they go out of business. That is a legitimate aim on their part, and I am not minimizing in any way the necessity or importance of commercial ends in a broadcasting system which must include private stations as well as public stations. But the system as a whole must be used not for commerical purposes entirely, but in the national interest.
And then there is a third requirement as far as we are concerned for any legislation which would be satisfactory to us. It is:
3.	That any regulatory board shall be accountable to and report directly to parliament. In our view it should not be a small official board of the nature of the board of transport commissioners. There should not be the kind of control over broadcasting which one sees exercised in Washington; the kind of official board which would be responsible to the government and which would have control over the regulating of both the private and the public elements of the system.
What we think should be in the legislation is a larger board, not composed of full time members. I have gone into this in some detail in debates on this matter previously in the house. The board, we think, should be one which would owe its responsibility directly to parliament and which would not be the agency of the government but an instrument of parliament. Then our fourth principle which we would like to see embodied in the legislation, is this:
4.	The retention of the existing system by which a few publicly-owned radio and television stations distribute through the facilities of a much larger number of private stations at least some of the C.B.C. produced "Canadian" programs. This means, of course, that the C.B.C. must be given power to own and operate at least some national networks and power to control the management of such networks.
Then also-and this is surely an essential principle in legislation of this kind-there must also be control over the private station. Without that control exercised in the public

Broadcasting
interest, because they are private stations operating for a profit-and I do not criticize them for that; they cannot go on without a profit-the temptation for them to affiliate with United States networks would be almost irresistible. If there were not that type of control over their activities exercised by a public board it would not be long before they were carrying exclusively and entirely United States programs. The reason for that is obvious. They could get those programs so much more cheaply than they could get a Canadian program. If it costs, say, $10,000 to produce a Canadian program, it might cost $30,000 or $40,000 to produce a similar type of program in the United States. But whereas a private station in Canada would have to pay a good deal to the C.B.C. for a Canadian program it might get a United States program for a fraction of that cost, because the cost of that program would in any case have been met in the large United States advertising market. Therefore the temptation for a private broadcaster to tie up with a United States network would be almost irresistible and that might represent an almost fatal blow to the Canadian national broadcasting system.
Ten o'clock.

I can finish in one minute. The fifth principle, Mr. Chairman, is this:
5.	There must be enforceable regulations by which any private network and any private station affiliated to such a private network shall be required to maintain programming standards which shall not be very different from those of the private stations affiliated to C.B.C. networks. This relates to what I have just been saying.
Then, finally, and this relates to the omission in the resolution to which I have already drawn attention:
6.	The necessary financial support for the C.B.C. should be provided from public moneys on a long term basis so that in addition to its earnings from commercial operations which are essential the C.B.C. shall be assured of the necessary funds with which to provide satisfactory national programming services. And that, of course, must be in addition to its income from commercial operations. Without the assurance of a minimum of income-and perhaps there should also be a maximum placed on the income-it would be difficult to see how they could effectively plan ahead. There is no suggestion in the resolution that this is going to be done.
I leave this thought with the minister in closing my remarks on this matter at the resolution stage. Would it not be better at
[Mr. Pearson.1
this stage to introduce a supplementary estimate covering C.B.C. operations to ensure that the work could be continued in the coming year and then introduce this bill? After first reading it could be submitted to a committee where it could be given the kind of examination to which it is entitled and thus ensure that we do not rush it through without careful consideration and without giving the house an opportunity to fully discuss a measure of such far-reaching importance to national development as this is. I am sure no hon. member of this committee wants to see the matter treated in that way but I am afraid that in the closing days of this session this very important question will not be given the consideration to which it is entitled if we are not extremely careful.
Progress reported.
